input:
Mara — 9:12 AM
morning, quick update on the Bellwether table cover. we opened the folded edge yesterday and found a second layer of plain linen under the blue wool, not another patch. The wool is brittle along the west border, but the center still flexes. I took photos with the scale and color card; they're in the restoration folder, under April 18.

Jonah — 9:19 AM
thanks, Mara. I looked at the close-ups. Is that pale line near the corner a stitch channel or a crease? In the room photo it looks straight, but the detail shot seems to bend toward the fringe. I don't want us calling it a seam until we can check it under the scope.

Leila — 9:27 AM
I think it's a crease, though I'm not certain. The linen layer has a narrow fold there and the wool nap changes direction at about the same point. The old inventory says “blue border repaired,” with no date or thread description. Could be referring to this area, could be another repair entirely.

Mara — 9:34 AM
that's how I read it too. We haven't lifted the wool anywhere else, since the adhesive residue gets powdery when the room is dry. The humidifier log shows 46% yesterday afternoon and 42% overnight, so I paused before putting any weight on the edge.

Nico — 9:43 AM
For context, the back is supported on washed cotton muslin, pinned to the padded board at 6 cm intervals. There are 3 loose pins along the short side, but none under the damaged border. The board is level, and the cover hasn't moved since we brought it in on Monday.

Priya — 9:51 AM
I checked the thread samples from the storage envelope. The blue one is probably wool, not silk, but the label just says “border, 1978?” with a question mark. The cream thread has a synthetic shine. We shouldn't assume either sample came from this cover, even though they're in the same envelope.

Jonah — 10:03 AM
One thing: the fringe is still attached at both ends, but the middle 11 cm is loose. I counted 14 visible warp ends there. A few are tucked under the folded linen, and I can't tell yet whether they were stitched down or just caught in the fold.

Leila — 10:11 AM
Mara, could you add one image with the ruler parallel to the border? The current ruler crosses it at an angle, which makes the gap look wider than it may be. No rush if the cover's already stable; I'd rather have a repeatable view than another close-up without a reference.

Mara — 10:18 AM
yep, I'll do that after the room settles. The north window was open for the delivery this morning, and the sensor went from 45% to 39% in about 20 minutes. I closed it and moved the air monitor closer, but I'm waiting on a steady reading before I bring the board out.

Tess — 10:31 AM
I found the 2009 treatment note in the blue binder. It says the cover was vacuumed through a screen, then wrapped in acid-free tissue; there isn't a diagram of the border. A later note mentions “loose edge” but doesn't say which side. The binder was stored flat, so the page isn't curled or missing.

Nico — 10:42 AM
For the record, the residue is on the linen, not obviously on the wool. Under magnification it looks like tiny amber flakes, but they could be old adhesive, sizing, or something transferred from the backing. I haven't taken a sample. The flakes are concentrated within about 2 cm of the fold.

Priya — 10:54 AM
Could we also log the room readings with each photo set? The room sheet has 43% at 9:00 and 41% at 10:00, while the portable meter read 44% beside the board. Those devices may not match exactly. It'd help if we note which one we're using instead of merging them.

Mara — 11:06 AM
yes. I added the meter ID to the photo notes and retook the border image straight-on. The 14 warp ends are easier to see now, but the folded linen still covers the last two. I haven't changed the support or touched the thread, and the cover is staying on the board for now.

Jonah — 11:17 AM
The close-up makes the pale line look less like a seam to me, but that's still tentative. There's a small shadow at the point where the line turns. If it's just a crease, the shadow could be from the fold; if it's a stitch channel, it might be the edge of the old thread. We need a better angle.

Leila — 11:29 AM
I can bring the low-angle lamp after lunch. We used it on the green runner last month, and it showed the direction of the pile without heating the textile. I'll check the bulb first, since the spare was flickering last week, and keep the lamp at least 40 cm from the cover.

Tess — 11:41 AM
Just a reminder that the handling sheet calls for two people if we move the board, even a short distance. The corridor is clear now, but the threshold by the photo room is raised, and one wheel on the trolley catches there. We can leave the cover in the workroom until the image set is done.

Mara — 11:52 AM
before we plan the next look, could someone confirm the order you'd use if the humidity stays between 42% and 46% this afternoon? Specifically, should we take the low-angle photos first and then examine the fold under magnification, or wait until the readings are steadier before either step? I haven't lifted the linen or sampled the flakes, and I'm not asking to move the board yet.

Nico — 12:04 PM
I can be there at 1:30 with the small scope and the color card. I'll bring the spare battery too; the scope shut off once during the curtain inspection. If the lighting changes the blue in the photos, we should keep the first set rather than replacing it, so there's a record of both conditions. :thumbsup:

input:
Mara: Morning, everyone. I’ve moved the blue silk banner to the padded table by the north windows. The room is holding at 20 degrees Celsius and 48 percent relative humidity.

Jon: Thanks. I checked the monitor at 8:15, and those readings match the overnight log. The west-side sensor is still a little slower to settle after the door opens.

Priya: The banner’s face is up, with the lettering panel supported on the foam roll. I’ve left the loose fringe in place rather than trying to straighten it.

Eli: I photographed the front and back before moving anything. The small tear near the lower right corner is about 3.5 centimeters, and there are two older stitch lines beside it.

Mara: I’ve added those images to the conservation folder, along with the close-up of the faded red border. The scale is visible in each detail shot.

Jon: The blue dye looks fairly even under the north-window light, but the fold along the top edge is much darker. I’ve noted the lighting conditions on the worksheet.

Priya: I tested the surface with the soft brush on the lowest setting. There’s loose dust along the top hem, but no visible fibers came away during that pass.

Eli: The backing fabric has three small areas of thinning around the center seam. I marked their locations on the diagram, using the lettering panel as the reference point.

Mara: For today’s work plan, we’re keeping to the dry surface cleaning and documentation. I’ve put the humidification materials on the side cart, not on the table.

Jon: That cart has the blotter, spun polyester, and the clean glass weights. I checked the labels, and the weights are all wrapped so they won’t touch the silk directly.

Priya: The fringe measures between 11 and 13 centimeters across the lower edge. A few ends are tangled, though I haven’t separated or trimmed any of them.

Eli: I found the inventory card in the gray folder. It calls the piece a “procession banner,” but it doesn’t give a maker or an exact date.

Mara: The card also lists a storage tube from the east cabinet. I checked that shelf this morning; the tube is there, with its paper label facing outward.

Mara: thanks, everyone. i'll send the polite decline with those two alternatives after Jo shares the public contact link. nothing's booked yet, and if Rowan replies with dates, we'll check the calendar and staffing before responding.

Hey team — I’m putting together next month’s local history newsletter, and I’m looking at the old Riverside footbridge for our short “Then and Now” feature. The county opened it in 1936, and it connected the mill district with the bus stop on Alder Street. A few readers have mentioned that people used to gather there on summer evenings, but I haven’t found anything in the archive that confirms it.

I’ve got a photo from the 1950s that shows a small crowd by the railing, though there’s no date or note on the back. I’m thinking we could pair it with a recent photo from the same spot and ask readers to share memories. We should probably be clear that the gathering story is still unconfirmed, rather than presenting it as fact. If anyone has a clipping, family photo, or a name for someone who might remember the bridge, that’d be really helpful.

Does anyone know whether the historical society has a better-dated copy of that photo, or another source about how the bridge was used? I can send the image around if that helps.

Mara: Quick heads-up: the April issue of the Mill Creek History Notes is stuck because our scan of the 1912 flood map is too faint to read the street names. The archive catalog lists it as “Mill Creek and East Ward, drainage plan, 1912,” box 8, folder 14. I’ll ask what equipment they use before we send anyone over.

Leila: I have a photo from the 2018 exhibit, but the lower-left corner is covered by the display frame. You can make out Alder Street and the old tram loop, though. I’ll put it in the shared folder so we have something to compare against the faint scan.

I don’t want to guess in print.

Theo: My grandmother kept a neighborhood scrapbook with a clipping about the flood works. I can look tonight. She labeled things by year, but the 1911 and 1913 pages are mixed together, so it might take a while. I’ll check for a caption or a street name that matches the map.

Nadia: I found the 1913 council minutes online. They mention a “channel cut beneath the wool mill” and a dispute over who would pay for the retaining wall. The minutes don’t quote the map note, so that’s useful context, but I wouldn’t treat it as proof of what the handwriting says.

Owen: For reference, the mill building was on the west side of Alder, near the footbridge that was removed in 1964. The flood map’s north arrow is tilted, which is why the river seems to run east in our draft caption. I can check the orientation against the Sanborn sheet when I’m at the archive tomorrow.

Mara: I’ve added the current draft caption to the folder. It reads: “A drainage plan for Mill Creek, 1912, showing a new channel below the wool mill.” Please don’t edit that line yet; I’m keeping it visible so we can see exactly which claim needs checking. The issue also has a short piece on the 1927 station clock.

Priya: I can ask the library’s digitization desk whether they have a camera stand and raking light. Last winter, they photographed the 1898 school ledger without pressing it flat. If that’s still possible, we could request just this sheet, rather than booking a full archive visit.

Jonas: The survey office says the map is mounted, not bound, and they can photograph it at the archive table next Wednesday. They don’t have a high-resolution file already. Their estimate is $18 for a digital copy, and we’d need to credit the county records room in the caption.

Leila: I’ve uploaded the exhibit photo as “flood-map-detail-2018.jpg.” It’s 2.4 MB, so it should be clear enough for comparison, but not for printing. The visible lettering under the frame looks like “channel below the mill”; I can’t tell whether there’s room for “new” or “old” before it.

Theo: Found the scrapbook clipping. The Mill Creek Gazette dated June 6, 1913, says residents objected to “the newly cut channel below the wool mill.” That sounds relevant, but it’s a newspaper report from a year after the map. I’ll scan the whole clipping tonight so we can quote it accurately and include the date.

Nadia: Nice find. Maybe the newsletter can say the map note is difficult to read and separately mention the 1913 report, rather than resolving the word from context. The neighborhood oral-history transcript from Mrs. Bell also calls it a new channel, but she was recalling events decades later. I’ll locate the page number if we want to cite that too.

Mara: That seems like a careful way to handle it. I still need help deciding whether we should hold the map caption for a week or use the cautious wording in this issue. The printer needs final pages Thursday afternoon, and the April issue is already a day behind because the station-clock photo arrived late.

Owen: I can go to the archive Wednesday morning and check the north arrow, street labels, and handwriting in person. If they let me take notes, I’ll write down what’s legible without filling in any gaps. Someone else could proof the 1927 clock piece while I’m there; its caption has the station’s opening date as 1904.

Priya: I called the digitization desk. They can photograph the mounted map on Thursday, but the file won’t be ready before Friday. The library might allow a quick reference photo during the visit, though they haven’t confirmed that yet. I’ll bring the request form and ask whether the $18 county copy is the faster option.

Mara: Could two people help with this? One person to compare the map against the Sanborn sheet and one to proof the clock article by noon tomorrow would be great. Please reply here if you’re available. I’ll keep the current caption in the draft until we know what the archive can provide, and I’ll send the printer a timing update tonight.

input:
lena: hey all, starting a thread for the May trip so we stop losing details in texts. We’re looking at May 22–27, driving from Portland to Vancouver and then over to Victoria. It’s six of us: Ravi and me, Noah (9), Mira (5), my mom Diane, and Priya. Nothing is booked yet except our aquarium tickets for Saturday.

ravi: I checked the calendar again, and Friday the 22nd is the first day we can all leave. I can take the Subaru, but with six people and bags it’ll be tight. The kids can share the back seat, and Diane says she’s fine in the passenger seat, but we still need to decide what to do with the luggage.

priya: I can bring my small duffel and a backpack, no hard suitcase. I’d rather not rent a second car unless we really need one. If we drive all the way, can we leave Portland by 7:00 a.m.? That should get us to the border before the afternoon traffic, though I’m not sure how much time to add for the crossing.

diane: I’m happy to leave early, but I don’t want to be rushed through breakfast. Could we pack sandwiches the night before and stop somewhere after we cross? I’d also like one proper stretch break for my knee. It’s okay on long drives as long as I get out and walk every couple of hours.

lena: For Vancouver, I found a hotel near Coal Harbour that has two queen beds and a pullout sofa. It’s $318 Canadian a night before tax, and parking is another $42 a night. The room says it sleeps six, but I haven’t called to check whether they count Mira as a full guest. Free cancellation ends May 8.

ravi: That’s more than I expected, but it’s walking distance to the aquarium and the seawall. The cheaper place by the airport is $229 a night, although we’d have to drive in and pay for parking downtown. I can call both hotels at lunch and ask about the bed setup, breakfast, and whether the parking price includes in-and-out privileges.

noah: is the aquarium really booked for 10:30 saturday? i want to see the penguins first and the jellyfish room. also can we get lunch there or should we bring snacks because i get hungry before noon

lena: Yes, the tickets are for 10:30 a.m. on Saturday, May 23. We can stay as long as we like, and I think there’s a café, but I haven’t checked the menu or prices. We should bring a couple of snacks in case the line is long. We’re not adding Science World this time; that would be too much for one day.

priya: On Sunday we could take the 11:00 ferry from Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay, then drive to Victoria. The sailing is about an hour and 35 minutes, but we’d need to arrive early with the car. I saw a fare estimate of $112 for the vehicle and two adults, plus $18 for each extra adult. Kids are less, but I didn’t get the exact amount.

ravi: Can you send the page you used? I saw a different total when I looked, and I’m not sure if it included the reservation fee. I’d rather book a specific sailing than risk lining up, especially with the kids and the bags. We need to leave enough time to check out of the hotel and get to Tsawwassen too.

lena: Here’s what I have so far for the middle of the trip:
1. Friday, May 22: drive Portland to Vancouver; check in and have an easy dinner.
2. Saturday, May 23: aquarium at 10:30; keep the afternoon open for the seawall or a rest.
3. Sunday, May 24: check out, ferry to Victoria, and pick up groceries on the way to the hotel.

priya: I like keeping Sunday light. The hotel in Victoria is a guesthouse near Cook Street Village, $274 Canadian a night for a family suite. It has a small kitchenette and breakfast is not included. They have one parking space per room, but the listing says we have to confirm the Subaru’s height because the garage clearance is low.

diane: The kitchenette would help, and I can make oatmeal for the kids if there’s a pot and bowls. I don’t need a fancy breakfast. Can you ask if the suite is on the ground floor? Stairs are manageable, but I’d rather not carry my suitcase up two flights if there’s another option.

ravi: I messaged the guesthouse this morning. They said the suite is on the second floor, but there’s an elevator. They haven’t confirmed the garage height yet; they asked for the vehicle model, so I sent Subaru Outback, 2021. They said they’ll reply by tomorrow. Cancellation is free until May 12.

lena: For Monday, May 25, the kids want the Royal BC Museum and the harbour. The museum is open until 5, but I can’t tell if we’ll need timed tickets. We could go in the morning, have lunch nearby, and leave the afternoon for Beacon Hill Park if the weather’s decent. No need to cram in Butchart Gardens too.

noah: can we go to the park with the goats? my friend said there are goats at beacon hill and i want to see them. also i want to bring my soccer ball but it might be too big for the car

priya: Beacon Hill has a petting zoo, but their site says it opens seasonally, so we should check the hours for that week. I can bring a small ball instead of the full-size one. For the museum, I didn’t see timed entry on the ticket page, but I only looked quickly. Maybe someone can verify before we buy anything.

diane: Tuesday the 26th could be a slower day. I’d like to walk around the Inner Harbour in the morning and sit somewhere for coffee. If everyone wants to see another garden or shop, I can take a break at the hotel and meet up later. I don’t want the schedule to assume I’m doing every activity.

ravi: Agreed. We should also work out the return route for Wednesday, May 27. The ferry from Victoria back to Tsawwassen is about 1 hour and 35 minutes, then it’s a long drive to Portland. There’s a Coho ferry to Port Angeles, but that adds a border crossing and a different route. I haven’t compared the prices or departure times yet.

lena: I’m leaning toward returning through Tsawwassen because it’s the route we already know, but I’m open to the Coho if it saves a meaningful amount of driving. We should plan a real meal and a break on the way home, not just hope the kids sleep. I can take the first driving shift if we leave early.

priya: I can handle the food list and bring a cooler, but we should agree on how many hotel nights we’re paying for. I counted two in Vancouver and three in Victoria, so five nights total. If we decide to add a night in Vancouver, that changes the ferry day and the hotel price. I don’t think we’ve agreed to that.

diane: Five nights works for me. Please don’t book a room with only one bathroom without checking first; that’s important with six people getting ready in the morning. I can share with Priya if the suite has two separate sleeping areas, but I’d like to know the actual layout before we pay a deposit.

ravi: I’ll put the booking details in one place once we hear from the hotels. For now, we have the aquarium tickets, but no hotel, ferry, museum, or garden tickets. The main open things seem to be the car space, exact room setup, and the return ferry. Tell me if I missed something.

lena: Specific question for everyone: should I try to reserve the larger Vancouver hotel and the Tsawwassen ferry first, or wait until we confirm the Victoria suite’s garage clearance and room layout? We have $1,600 set aside for lodging and ferries before food, and I don’t want to spend it in the wrong order. Please share what you’d prioritize, and flag anything I’ve got wrong.

input:
Mara: hey all, quick update on the August trip. we're still looking at Aug 8–13, and there are six of us if Ben joins.

Eli: I checked flights from Albany to Bangor again. the nonstop isn't running those dates, so we'd have one connection in Philadelphia.

Nina: the connection I saw was 58 minutes, which feels tight with the kids and carry-ons. there's another option through Baltimore with 1h 42m.

Mara: yeah, I'd rather not sprint through Philly. the Baltimore flight lands at 2:15 p.m., if that schedule hasn't changed since yesterday.

Ben: I'm still a maybe, just waiting on my work calendar. I should know by Friday, not promising yet.

Jo: lodging update: the cottage in Ellsworth is available Aug 8–13, but the owner only holds it until Thursday at 6.

Eli: it's $1,680 total before the cleaning fee, and there are three bedrooms, one bathroom, and a pullout couch.

Nina: I asked about linens. the owner said sheets and towels are included, but beach towels aren't, so we should pack those.

Mara: I read the reviews again. two people mention steep stairs to the bedrooms, so that's worth knowing for Dad's knee.

Jo: Dad said, “stairs are fine if I can take them slowly,” but he doesn't want to carry luggage up.

Eli: there's also a motel in Bar Harbor for $2,040. it has two rooms, but breakfast is included and it's walkable to dinner.

Nina: I don't think we need to decide the motel today. the cottage has a kitchen, which could help with breakfast and lunches.

Mara: agreed. here's the loose plan, not a reservation or anything yet:
1. arrive in Bangor Friday afternoon and pick up the rental van.
2. stop for groceries in Ellsworth before checking in.
3. keep Saturday flexible, depending on weather and how everyone feels.

Jo: the grocery store closes at 9, according to its site. if we land late, we can get a few basics at the airport instead.

Eli: airport shop prices are rough, though. I can bring coffee, oatmeal, and the kids' snack bars from home.

Nina: please do, and I'll bring the small cooler. it fits behind the passenger seat, but not in the overhead bin.

Ben: do we know if the rental van has a second driver fee? I'm fine driving, but want to check before we book.

Mara: the quote shows no extra driver fee for a spouse, but I'm not sure it applies to siblings. I'll call tomorrow.

Jo: Dad and I can drive from Portland if flights get too expensive. our car fits four with luggage, not six, obviously.

Eli: current flights are $386 each with a carry-on. checked bags are another $40 each way, so I think we should pack light.

Nina: the kids can share one checked bag, but I need room for their rain jackets. forecast is impossible this far out, obviously.

Mara: Acadia's timed vehicle reservations aren't posted for our dates yet. I set a reminder for the first week of June.

Eli: Cadillac Summit Road reservations usually sell out quickly, but we don't have to do that on the first morning.

Jo: yes, Dad wants to see the coast, not spend the whole trip in the van. maybe one scenic drive is enough.

Nina: I bookmarked the Jordan Pond loop. it's 3.3 miles, and the page calls it moderate; we can turn back whenever.

Mara: good. Dad's knee is better than last spring, but let's keep the walking plans optional and not stack hikes.

Ben: if I come, I can take the kids for the tide pools while you all do the shorter loop.

Eli: tide pool timing depends on the actual low tide, so I'll check the chart when the dates get closer.

Jo: there's a small beach near the cottage too, but reviews say the water's cold even in August. bring sweatshirts.

Nina: I found a lobster place in Southwest Harbor with outdoor tables. they don't take reservations for groups under eight.

Mara: that's fine. with six people we can just wait, unless Ben's partner comes too; still not sure about that.

Ben: Casey probably can't make the whole week. they're checking whether they can join for Saturday night only.

Eli: if Casey comes just Saturday, the cottage still has the pullout couch. I asked the owner and got no answer yet.

Jo: for meals, I'd rather not plan every dinner. let's pick two places and keep the other nights easy at the house.

Nina: I can make pasta the first night if we get in before 7. otherwise sandwiches are totally fine.

Mara: the cottage listing says check-in is 4 p.m. and checkout is 10 a.m. I'm asking if an earlier bag drop is possible.

Eli: don't count on early access. we can leave the bags in the van and walk around Ellsworth if there's time.

Jo: the van quote is $612 for five days, including taxes, but it doesn't include fuel or the optional damage coverage.

Mara: I haven't compared the coverage details yet. please don't book it until I confirm the sibling driver question too.

Nina: understood. I'll keep the cooler and snack list in the shared note, not buy anything this week.

Ben: I'll add my work update Friday. no need to count me in for costs until I confirm.

Eli: parking at the cottage is listed for two cars. if Jo and Dad drive up separately, we'll need to ask about a third.

Jo: we can leave our car at the Portland hotel and ride up with you, if we decide to fly.

Mara: the hotel is still just a backup for Thursday night. it's $174, cancellable until Aug 6, and breakfast costs extra.

Nina: I put the flight options, cottage link, van quote, and tide chart in the shared folder. nothing's booked yet.

Mara: thanks, everyone. next check-in after Ben hears about work and I call the rental place. dates are still Aug 8–13 🙂

Joel: maybe note that the covers aren't impact protection. the 1100 sleeve has a small tear at the seam, about 4 cm long, so i'd use the gray sleeve for transport and keep the torn one on the shelf until we stitch it.

Mira: i'll add that to the gear list, but not to the shop reply unless they ask about transport. we don't know how they'll move it, and the request was just for the carbon foil and mast for photos.

Joel: the cones are fine, just keep them out of the marked access path. last month someone set a sign across that entrance and we had to move the whole table. no need to stake anything into the sand if the wind stays up.

Mira: i'll check with the shop about the alternative and ask whether they're okay with the aluminum mast and larger wing. if they need the exact carbon setup for the shot, we'll politely decline rather than promise something we can't provide.

Joel: i'd stick with the 80 cm mast as the suggested alternative. the 65 cm one has a different plate shim in place, and we'd have to re-check the setup anyway. we can mention it only if they ask for a shallow-water option.

Mira: sounds good. i'll send the polite no on the carbon foil, explain briefly that we're checking the joint, and offer the 105-liter board with the aluminum freeride kit as an alternative. i'll ask them to confirm whether that would suit their shoot.

input:
Mara: Thanks for the detailed ride notes, Jules. Your point about the front truck feeling twitchy on the cracked path is useful. We’d been testing on smooth pavement, so we weren’t seeing that same movement. I’m pulling the setup notes into this thread so we can compare the changes clearly.

Jules: Yep, the rough section by the old rail bridge is where I noticed it most. At about 18 mph, the board wandered when I crossed the seams. It wasn’t a speed wobble, exactly; it just took more small corrections than my other setup. The rear felt planted the whole time.

Mara: Got it. You also mentioned that the board was easier to pump after you changed the front bushings. Which ones did you swap in? I have the stock 90a barrels listed on your original build sheet, but I don’t want to assume those were still on the board during the ride.

Jules: I put in the 87a roadside bushings from the spare kit, with the stock roadside washers. The boardside barrels are still 90a. I tightened the kingpin nut about a quarter turn after the first run, then backed it off a little when the return felt slow.

Devin: That’s a helpful detail. The truck has a 50-degree baseplate, and a softer roadside bushing can make the steering feel more responsive without changing the baseplate angle. A quarter turn can also be a noticeable adjustment on that setup. Did you keep the same wheel wells and risers as before?

Jules: Yes, same 1/8-inch risers and the 70 mm wheels. I didn’t get any wheel bite, even when I leaned hard through the parking-lot turns. The wheels are the 78a ones, not the 80a set from the photos. I should’ve called that out earlier.

Mara: No worries, that’s exactly the kind of context we need. I’ll update the ride log to show the 78a wheels and the bushing change. Your other comment was that the deck felt comfortable underfoot but flexed more than you expected near the rear bolts. Did you notice that loaded or just while carrying it?

Jules: Loaded, with my backpack on. I’m around 82 kg, and the pack was maybe 6 kg. I felt a little extra give when I shifted back to push, but there wasn’t a creak or any visible separation around the inserts. The deck is the 38-inch maple one with the shallow rocker.

Inez: Thanks, Jules. That’s a useful distinction. The 38-inch deck has a longer wheelbase than the sample we used for the product photos, and that can change how flex feels even when the layup is the same. Could you share which mounting holes you used? The inner pair changes the wheelbase by about half an inch.

Jules: I used the outer holes, for the longer wheelbase. I prefer the extra room for my stance, especially on the bike path. My front foot sits just behind the front bolts, and my back foot is a few inches ahead of the tail. I didn’t measure the exact distance.

Mara: That matches the build sheet. I’m replying to your overall feedback here: we can describe the deck as having noticeable flex under a loaded stance, but I wouldn’t call that a defect based on one ride. We should keep the wording specific to what you felt and avoid implying that you tested it with a heavier load.

Jules: That works for me. I wasn’t trying to say it’s unsafe or that the deck is damaged. It felt comfortable, and the flex didn’t bother me while cruising. I just expected it to feel stiffer because the product page calls the maple layup “firm and supportive.”

Devin: Fair point about that wording. “Firm and supportive” doesn’t give much context for rider weight or wheelbase. We could add a note that perceived flex varies with stance, load, and mounting position. I’d keep your quote as feedback, though, since it explains what led to the expectation.

Mara: Agreed. I’ll include the quote in the internal notes and suggest a more specific line for the page, not replace the current copy yet. There’s also your note about the grip tape collecting grit near the tail. Was that after the wet ride on Saturday, or did it happen during the dry test?

Jules: Dry test. I brushed the deck off before I started, but little bits of gravel stuck to the tape after the path. They came off with a stiff nylon brush. The tape still felt grippy under my shoes, and the edges weren’t lifting. I haven’t ridden it in rain.

Inez: Good to know. The tape is the coarse black sheet from the current batch, and we haven’t changed the grit size on that run. I’ll note that it held small gravel but cleaned up with a brush. Since you haven’t ridden in rain, let’s leave wet-weather grip out of the summary.

Owen: I checked the hardware list against Mara’s notes: stainless 1.5-inch bolts, 1/8-inch risers, and the standard 50-degree trucks. Nothing in the spec sheet conflicts with Jules’s setup. The photos show the 80a wheels, so we should label them as studio photos rather than use them to identify the ride configuration.

Mara: 1. Ride notes to carry forward: 78a, 70 mm wheels; 87a roadside bushings with 90a boardside barrels; stock roadside washers; outer mounting holes; and no reported wheel bite. 2. Deck feedback: comfortable, with noticeable flex under a backpack load. 3. Grip feedback: gravel collected on a dry path and brushed off; no rain test.

Rae: Thanks, Jules, for taking the time to write this up and for being precise about what you did and didn’t test. We’ll use the setup details when we review the product-page wording. If you get another chance to ride the board, the same route with the original bushings would make a useful comparison, but there’s no pressure to do another test.

input:
hey folks, quick bench update on the little temperature display. i soldered the header pins onto the sensor board last night, and mounted the screen on a scrap piece of acrylic. the screen is 0.96 inch, 128 by 64, and the sensor is a bme280 i had in the parts drawer. i powered it from the usb port on my laptop, not the bench supply, so the wiring is still pretty simple.

the first reading came up about 1.8 degrees c higher than the room thermometer, but both were sitting in different spots on the desk. i'll leave them side by side for a while before i change anything. the display refreshes every two seconds right now, which is probably more often than it needs to.

i haven't put the board in an enclosure yet. the acrylic is just a temporary mount, and one corner is a little rough from the handsaw. i have a small project box here, but it may be too shallow once the usb cable is plugged in. does anyone know if these boxes usually have enough room for a right-angle cable? i can measure the clearance after work and post it here. no photos yet; i forgot to bring the phone stand to the bench.

Jon: please don't drill until we hold the board and display in place together. the display ribbon bends toward the sensor connector, and i think the current notch may pinch it if we close the lid too tightly.

Eli: about the sketch, i pushed the version with the slower screen refresh. it waits 250 ms between readings now, so the numbers shouldn't flicker as much. i haven't changed the alarm threshold or the pin assignments.

Nia: thanks, i saw that commit. i'll bring the USB cable so we can load it from my laptop, but let's save the current version first in case the new refresh timing causes a weird display issue.

Jon: i can make a quick wiring diagram at the bench. the current paper one has the sensor OUT line crossing the 5v line, and it looks like a connection even though it's just a crossing.

Mara: please do, and put the board revision on it. mine says rev B near the mounting holes, but the old notes don't mention a revision, so we should keep the updated sheet with the enclosure.

Nia: i can also bring the calipers. the enclosure wall is about 2 mm thick from my rough measurement, and i want to check that before we decide how long the screws should be.

Jon: sounds good. i've got short M3 screws and a few longer ones in the parts case. we can compare them against the standoffs instead of cutting anything at the bench.

Mara: perfect. let's aim to finish the wiring check and fit test, not rush into sealing the case. if we find a problem with the ribbon or sensor lead, we can note it and leave the lid off.

Eli: agreed. i'll bring a notebook and write down the supply voltage, current reading, and any changes to the wiring. then we can compare those with the notes from the loose-board test.

Nia: and i'll take a photo of the final layout before we move anything. that helped last time when the display connector got turned around, and we had to work out which way it had been sitting.

Jon: see you all thursday. i'll bring the labels and diagram pencil, and i'll check that the bench light is working when i arrive. 🙂

input:
Mara: hey all, quick question about the oct 18 film night at the harbor room: should we move doors from 6:30 to 6:15 and the film from 7:00 to 6:45? The library has a youth poetry event ending at 6, so a few families might come straight over. We haven't changed the listing yet.

Dev: i checked with the venue this morning. We can get in at 5:45 either way, but the custodian needs the room cleared by 9:30. The movie is 94 minutes, and with the intro + a short discussion we'd be done around 8:35 if we start at 6:45. 7:00 still fits too.

Inez: one wrinkle: the bus from east ridge gets to bay street at 6:28, then it's about a 7 min walk. Last month people were still finding seats after the welcome. If we start earlier, some folks could miss the first few minutes, unless we hold the intro til 7:00? not sure that solves it.

Cal: the youth event is in the room next door, not the library hall. Their coordinator told me, “we expect families to leave by 6:10, but a few may stay to stack chairs.” There's a shared lobby, so the noise could carry over while we're setting up. They aren't using our chairs.

Mara: thanks, that's useful. For context, our usual crowd is 25–35 people, and we have 32 chairs plus 8 folding ones in the storage closet. We haven't had to turn anyone away, but October's title has been getting more RSVPs than usual. I can bring the little sign-in table from home.

Jo: could we put the door sign outside the side entrance? The front path is partly blocked by the paving work, and last time two people went to the cafe entrance by mistake. Building staff said the side door is open until 7:15, but after that we need to meet late arrivals.

input:
Maya: The June film nights are on the calendar for the 6th, 13th, and 20th at the Eastside Library courtyard. Doors open at 6:30 p.m., and screenings start at 7:15. The library will keep its side entrance open until the first film begins.

Jonah: I checked the projector with Luis yesterday. The image is clear on the white screen from the back row, and the audio cable reaches the table without crossing the main walkway. We’ll bring the shorter extension cord as a backup.

Priya: The first film is *The Secret of Kells*, and the second is *Whale Rider*. We’re still waiting for the neighborhood group to confirm the title for the 20th, so the printed handout lists that slot as “community choice.”

Luis: The courtyard seats about 55 people comfortably. We have 36 folding chairs from the library and 12 from the recreation center, plus four benches along the garden wall. I’ll mark the uneven paving stones with small reflective strips before doors open.

Maya: The library asked us to keep the west gate clear because the evening book club uses that entrance. Their meeting ends at 6:45, so our welcome table will stay near the fountain until then. Afterward, we can move it beside the poster board.

Theo: Here’s the snack update: the bakery on Pine Street is donating 40 small rolls for each date, and the market has offered a crate of apples for June 6. We’ll have water in paper cups, with a labeled bin for compost and another for recycling.

Priya: I spoke with Ana at the neighborhood group. She said, “We’d rather have a film everyone can discuss than a surprise that needs a long introduction.” Their members are sending three suggestions by Friday; the 20th’s title is still open until we hear back.

Jonah: The rental screen is 12 feet wide and fits between the two courtyard lamps. Luis measured the space this morning, and there’s about three feet on either side for the speaker stands. We’ll test the setup again at 5:45 on the first night.

Maya: A few practical notes for volunteers:
1. Check people in at the fountain table and point out the accessible path along the east wall.
2. Keep the library’s front steps free of bags and chairs.
3. Bring a light jacket; the courtyard gets breezy after sunset.

Luis: The accessible path is paved, but there’s a narrow turn beside the herb beds. We’ll leave that corner open and put the sign on the fence rather than on the ground. The library has two portable lanterns we can use near the path.

Theo: I’ve updated the flyer with the three dates, the door time, and the library address. The print shop can have 60 copies ready on Wednesday. The digital version has a map link and a note that seating is first come, first served.

Priya: The school art club is making a small display of film posters for the courtyard wall. Their teacher, Mr. Chen, said the students can bring the pieces on June 6, but they’ll use removable clips so nothing gets attached to the brick.

Jonah: For sound, we’ll use the library’s two powered speakers and the mixer from the community center. The center’s equipment bag includes the right adapters, according to Denise. I’ve added fresh batteries for the remote to the supply list.

Maya: The rain plan is the library meeting room, which holds 42 people. The building manager needs an hour to switch the room layout, so we’ll post a weather update by noon on each screening day if rain looks likely. The films and start times stay the same.

Luis: I’ll bring the sign-in sheets, reflective tape, and a small first-aid kit. The library asked that we keep food outside the meeting room if we use the rain plan. We’ll put that note on the volunteer clipboard, along with the room’s capacity.

Theo: The youth center has offered to lend us two folding tables for the welcome area. I’ll pick them up Thursday afternoon and return them Saturday morning. They’re stored in the garage behind the center, and the caretaker has the key.

Priya: The first-night volunteer list has eight names, including two people who can stay through cleanup. We’ll collect the reusable cups and sort the cardboard after each screening. The library closes at 9:30, so we’ll aim to have the courtyard clear by 9:15.

Maya: That’s the current update for June. The schedule, setup notes, and volunteer details are in the shared folder, and the flyer is ready for printing. I’ll add the final June 20 title once the neighborhood group sends its suggestions.

input:
Maya: hey, thanks for the localization pass on the settings flow. i went through the feedback doc this morning and there are a few things i want to make sure we understand before we change strings. the French “Turn on alerts” note says it sounds like a permanent system setting, but this toggle only covers alerts for one project. do you think “Enable project alerts” is clear enough, or does that still read too technical?

Leo: yeah, i agree the scope is easy to miss. in the screenshot the project name is above the toggle, but it disappears on the narrow layout, so the string has to carry more of that meaning. maybe “Get alerts for this project” is more natural in French too? i haven't checked with Camille yet, and i don't want us to choose based on english alone.

Nina: one small thing from the German review: “Save changes” is currently “Änderungen speichern,” which is correct, but the reviewer says it feels abrupt beside the secondary action “Cancel.” they suggested “Änderungen übernehmen.” that can imply applying changes immediately though, and our save button only stores the draft until the user leaves the page. i'd keep the current wording unless we can check that nuance.

Maya: good catch, thanks. can we ask the reviewer for an alternative that keeps the draft meaning? also, please don't change the button in the branch yet. the feedback is helpful, but i think we need a bit more context on the screen-reader label before deciding whether “Save” is the issue or the pairing with “Cancel.”

Omar: i tested the screen reader on build 4.18.2 with French and German selected. it announces “Save changes, button” and then reads the unsaved-changes hint below it. the hint isn't linked to the button, though, so a user who tabs directly to the action may not hear that the save is only a draft. i'm not sure if adding that to the accessible name is the right fix, since it could get pretty long.

Leo: could we use “Save draft” for the accessible name but leave the visible button as “Save changes”? i know that means different strings in the resource file, and it might not match our usual pattern. another option is linking the hint with aria-describedby. do we know if that works consistently with VoiceOver and NVDA, or would it repeat the hint when people move through the form?

Priya: i can check the aria-describedby behavior, but i only have a Windows test device this week, so i can't confirm VoiceOver myself. also, the hint says “Changes are saved when you leave this page,” which is not quite right: they're saved as a draft when you click the button, and leaving the page is a separate step. i'd suggest we review that source sentence before translating it again.

hey, quick barcode scan update from receiving. we tried the new handhelds on lanes 2 and 3 this morning and the first pass was a little slower than the old units. lane 2 scanned 184 cartons with 7 misses; lane 3 got 201 cartons with 5 misses. most misses were on labels near the bottom seam, where the wrap was folded over the last digit. the team wiped the lenses around 10:30 and scans improved after that, so dust might've been part of it too.

Leon — 8:15 AM: I noticed it on lane 4 around 7:40. The first scan beeped, and the scanner screen showed the carton ID, but the dashboard stayed blank. I wrote down three examples before the next pallet arrived: BX-48192, BX-48197, and BX-48203.

Maya — 8:52 AM: That’s useful. Did the carton stay at the induction point for those 35 seconds, or had it already passed the diverter? I want to know whether the delay affects the physical routing or only what the receiving crew sees on screen.

Derek — 8:57 AM: It had passed the diverter and was waiting at the end of the belt. The lane light stayed green, and the carton went to the expected staging area. The crew held it there because the dashboard entry wasn’t visible yet.

Leon — 9:03 AM: I checked the other two IDs from my notes. BX-48192 appeared about 20 seconds after its scan, while BX-48197 appeared immediately on the second scan. BX-48203 is still in the dashboard history, but its event time is 7:51.

Priya — 9:08 AM: I’m seeing several brief spikes in AP-WH-07 latency between 7:35 and 8:05, but no full disconnect. The log records retries at 7:42 and 7:51. I can’t tell from this view whether those retries delayed scanner events or just routine status traffic.

Maya — 9:13 AM: Could you share the latency range and whether it overlaps those carton times? I’m not asking anyone to change the access point configuration yet. If the timing lines up, we can give support a focused set of examples instead of guessing.

Priya — 9:18 AM: The spikes reached 480–620 ms, with most readings under 90 ms. The 7:42 retry lines up with Leon’s first example; the 7:51 retry may line up with BX-48203. I don’t have a precise scan timestamp for that carton.

Derek — 9:24 AM: I found a photo of the lane 4 setup from yesterday’s cleanup. WS-14 is mounted above the belt, about 1.8 meters from the carton path, and the bracket doesn’t look loose. There’s a new metal guard beside the cable tray, installed Monday.

Leon — 9:29 AM: The guard is about 30 centimeters from the scanner cable, not the scanner head. It was added to keep empty totes from hitting the tray. I haven’t noticed the signal indicator flicker, but I can check the cable route during the next lull.

Maya — 9:35 AM: Please do, and don’t move the bracket while the lane is running. Also, can we get one clean comparison from lane 3 using the same Northstar label batch? That might tell us whether the delay follows the labels or stays with WS-14.

Derek — 9:42 AM: Lane 3 has the same supplier batch coming in after lunch. I can scan a few cartons there and record the dashboard times, then compare them with lane 4. I’ll use the carton IDs and minute-level timestamps, not photos of the labels.

Priya — 9:48 AM: I can pull the scanner event log for WS-14 if we have a 15-minute window. It includes received time and device time, but the display doesn’t show the carton ID in every row. Does 7:35–7:55 cover the examples well enough?

Maya — 9:53 AM: Yes, that window should cover the first reports. Please include the AP latency entries in the same export if that’s easy. We’re not sure yet that they’re related, and I’d rather keep the log review to those times.

Leon — 10:01 AM: I checked the cable route. It’s secured, the connector is fully seated, and there’s no visible damage. The status indicator stayed solid while I gently moved the cable at the strain relief. I didn’t unplug anything or change the scanner settings.

Derek — 10:07 AM: I’ve put a note on the lane board asking the crew to record the scan time and carton ID if the dashboard entry is delayed. I also told them to keep the carton in the expected staging area and call the floor lead if the route looks wrong.

Maya — 10:12 AM: Thanks, everyone. Could someone from support help us compare WS-14’s event timestamps with AP-WH-07’s latency around 7:42 and 7:51? We have a few delayed entries, but no confirmed routing error, and we haven’t changed any settings.

Priya — 10:17 AM: I’ll attach the limited log window and the three carton IDs to the support thread. I’ll label the times as approximate where we don’t have an exact scan timestamp. If they need a wider export, I’ll check with the floor lead first.

inez: i checked the basket before lunch. it had maple seeds, two bits of willow leaf, and a lot of fine string algae, mostly caught on the lower side. the basket wasn't packed tight, so i rinsed it in a bucket of pond water and put it back.

dev: on the water test, ph was 7.4 and the strip looked between 0 and 1 ppm for nitrite. nitrate was about 10 ppm. i might have held the strip in the light too long, though, so those are rough readings, not a new baseline.

mara: small maintenance list for next visit:
1. brush the algae from the shallow shelf, without scraping the liner.
2. check the pump basket again after the leaves drop.
3. look at the air stone; it was bubbling, but the bubbles seemed uneven on one side.

leo: i can bring the soft pond brush. last time it loosened the film without lifting the gravel, as long as i worked toward the drain and didn't press hard. i'll keep the brush separate from the patio scrubber.

inez: please don't brush the whole shelf in one go. there are two small snails near the flat rock, and i saw one tadpole under the ledge. we can leave that corner alone for now and do the open section only.

sam: good point. i saw the same snails on sunday, just below the water line. i didn't move them. the tadpole was still there when i left, but i couldn't tell if there were others farther under the ledge.

dev: the air pump noise is about the same as last month, a low hum with a brief rattle when it starts. the hose isn't kinked, and the plug stayed dry. i didn't open the housing because it was working normally after the first few seconds.

mara: one thing i noticed: the water was lower on the south edge than it looked from the path, but the stones were dry outside and there wasn't a wet patch around the pond. could just be the slight slope in that section.

tess: i checked the log photos from the past three saturdays. the level mark looks nearly unchanged in all of them, and the south edge has that same gap under the flat stone. i'll take another photo from the bench next time for comparison.

leo: the heron decoy is still by the shed, not beside the pond. i left it there because it kept falling over in the wind last week. no heron sightings since thursday, and the fish were visible when i walked around at dusk.

inez: for the plants, the yellow flag iris has one new leaf and no yellowing at the base. the water lily has two pads with small brown edges, but the rest look firm. i removed one loose, damaged pad that was already floating.

sam: i brought the clay pot with the dwarf rush back from the garage. the soil was damp but not soggy, and the roots weren't showing through the holes. i set it on the east shelf, where it doesn't block the skimmer.

dev: did anyone add barley straw this month? the mesh bag by the shed is still tied shut, so i assumed not. there's also a half-full bottle of pond conditioner on the lower shelf, but the label is hard to read.

mara: no straw added by me. i left the bag closed, and i haven't used the conditioner. the label says it was opened in april, though i can't make out the full date; let's check it before deciding whether it's still in date.

tess: i'll bring the small notebook and a fresh test strip pack on saturday. the old pack says use by october, and the lid hasn't been sealing properly. i'll leave the receipt in the garden folder so we know which pack is which.

input:
mara: hey all, quick update on the radio drama. the new episode is called “The Last Light at Pier Nine,” and we’re aiming for a 28-minute cut before the first table read on thursday. the harbor setting is working really well, especially the foghorn and the little radio shop.

eli: agreed. i listened to the rough mix on the bus this morning, and the bell over the shop door lands nicely before june hears the weather report. i put a note in the episode doc about letting that ring finish before we bring in the music.

mara: thanks! also, the arts council asked if we can add a two-minute announcement for their winter fundraiser right after the opening. they want the date, ticket link, and a thank-you to the ferry company in the same read. can someone take a look before i reply?

rohan: i get why they asked, and the fundraiser sounds worthwhile, but i don't think we can fit that announcement into this episode. the opening is already doing a lot of story work, and a separate promo there would interrupt june finding the broken transmitter.

mara: same concern from me. we promised a self-contained drama, not an ad slot, and the episode's opening is only about ninety seconds. i also don't want to promise a new version until we know whether the mix has room for another voice.

jules: could we just have the station host mention it while she's reading the forecast? that might feel less like a separate announcement. not sure if it would still be too much, though, since the host already has the ferry closure and the storm warning.

eli: i wouldn't add it to her forecast. the fundraiser isn't part of the story, and putting it in her mouth could make it sound like the fictional station is endorsing the event. we should keep her lines focused on the storm and the missing supply boat.

mara: yeah, good point. i'd like to decline politely and offer something useful instead. we could share the event details in our episode notes, if the council sends us the final link and approved wording. that keeps the audio cut intact.

rohan: that works for me. maybe also offer them a short mention in the listening guide, which goes out with the episode. we can say we're happy to include the date and ticket link there, but we can't promise a placement until the guide is laid out.

jules: +1 to the guide. just checking: do we have the final episode duration yet? the export i saw was 27:42, but it didn't have the last two room-tone fades or the end credits. those could push us a little over.

eli: not final yet. the harbor ambience is still being cleaned up, and i asked noah to soften the low rumble under the shop scene. he hasn't sent that pass back. i'd rather not quote a runtime to the council until the final master is checked.

mara: totally. i'll avoid mentioning a duration. here's a possible reply, not sent yet: “Thanks for thinking of the episode. We can't add a fundraiser announcement to the audio, because we're keeping this installment focused on the story. We can consider the event details for the episode notes and listening guide once you send the final link and wording.”

rohan: that reads kind and clear. maybe change “consider” to “include”? only if we're actually okay with doing it. if we still need to check the link and the guide layout, “consider” is safer and doesn't sound like a guarantee.

mara: good catch, let's keep “consider.” i can ask the council to send the link by monday so we have time to check it before the notes go to the web team. if it arrives later, we can still tell them we may not be able to fit it in.

jules: one small thing: their message asked for a thank-you to the ferry company too. should we say we can't include that in the episode, or leave it out of the reply unless they ask again? i don't want our alternative to accidentally sound like we agreed to thank the company.

eli: i'd mention that the audio announcement isn't possible, without listing every requested item. the episode notes can carry event information, but a thank-you isn't event information exactly. we could ask them to send the approved copy and then decide what fits the notes.

mara: agreed. i'll make sure the reply doesn't promise the ferry-company thank-you. plan for now:
1. keep the episode script and mix unchanged for the fundraiser request.

input:
Mara: Thanks for listening to “The Glass Harbor” and sending such detailed notes, Eli. I’m glad the storm sequence felt tense without making the radio crew sound like they’d suddenly become action heroes. That balance was tricky, especially once we added the damaged antenna and the ferry’s foghorn.

Eli: The atmosphere really worked for me. I could picture the wet windows and the green signal lamp in the station, and the pauses made the last transmission land. I did lose track of why Nessa stayed at the lighthouse after Tomas went back to the harbor, though. I thought she was supposed to leave with him.

Mara: That’s fair. In the earlier draft, Tomas asks her to come back, but Nessa says she needs to keep the lamp going until the second ferry clears the rocks. We cut that exchange for time and didn’t replace it clearly enough. I’ll bring the reason back into the scene, probably as a quick line before Tomas leaves.

Dev: I had the same question on my first listen. Also, the ticking sound under Nessa’s final report is excellent. We recorded it with the old kitchen timer from the studio, not a library effect, and the uneven tick gave the actor something to play against. It gets quieter when the batteries start to fail.

Mara: Nice catch, Dev. The timer detail was from our sound notes, but I wasn’t sure anyone would notice. Eli, was the ending confusing too, or did it feel like Nessa actually reached the mainland? We wanted the last line to leave that uncertain, not confirm what happened to her.

Eli: The ending read as uncertain to me, in a good way. I heard the ferry horn fade and then the station receiver click off, but I couldn’t tell whether the voice on the final signal was Nessa or the harbor operator. The ambiguity felt intentional; the lighthouse question felt like I’d missed a practical detail.

Mara: That’s exactly the distinction we hoped would come through. The final voice is meant to stay unidentified, and we’ll keep the receiver click as the last sound. I’ll make the lighthouse choice clearer without adding an answer about who sent the signal. Thanks for putting your finger on the difference.

Jo: One other small note: the transition from the harbor office to the lighthouse came in pretty fast. The bell rings, Tomas says, “I’m going to find her,” and then he’s already outside in the rain. I liked the urgency, but a half-second of the door latch or his coat might help the location change register.

Mara: Good point. We can try the latch and one step into the rain before the next line, then listen for whether it slows the chase. I don’t want to add a whole walk across town; the scene should still feel like he’s making a rushed decision after hearing the second warning bell.

Dev: We have a clean latch recording from the booth door, but it sounds heavier than the lighthouse station door. I can record the smaller prop door this afternoon and layer in the rain bed from scene four. The rain there has the same close, tinny roof sound, so it should connect without suggesting a new location.

Mara: Please do a quick version, Dev, and label it “lighthouse latch alt” so we can compare it with the current cut. Keep the old transition in the session too. I’d rather hear both versions before changing the mix, especially because the bell and the coat movement are already close together in the left channel.

Eli: I also wondered if Tomas’s “I’m going to find her” line should be less certain. He’s heard the warning, but he doesn’t know Nessa stayed at the lighthouse until the ferry passed. Maybe he says he’s checking the station instead? That would fit the moment without revealing that he knows where she is.

Mara: I see what you mean, though I’d like to preserve the urgency in that line. Tomas has already tried the harbor office and got no answer, so “find her” is a guess rather than a claim that he knows her location. Let’s listen with the clearer lighthouse line first and see whether the existing dialogue still feels misleading.

Jo: For reference, the numbering in the script notes currently jumps from 2 to 4. I think section 3 was the paragraph about the ferry schedule, which got moved into the production appendix. It’s not a problem for the audio, but we should fix the numbering before the cast gets the revised pages.

Mara: Thanks, Jo. I’ll check the appendix against the latest script and restore the number if that section is still there. The ferry schedule matters because the second crossing leaves at 11:40, and we mention the time twice in the dialogue. I don’t want the printed notes to imply we cut that detail from the episode.

Dev: I’ll send the latch alt and a separate version with the rain one decibel lower. Right now the roof sound masks the receiver click if I raise the latch too much. I won’t replace the existing mix; I’ll put both tests in the review folder with the scene-four rain bed noted in the filenames.

Eli: That all makes sense. The episode’s strongest bits for me are the small sounds—the timer, the foghorn arriving late, and Nessa tapping the receiver twice before she speaks. Those details made the station feel lived in. The lighthouse explanation should be enough to make her choice legible without spelling out what happens after the final signal.

Mara: Agreed. I’ll make the one-line story change, and we’ll keep the uncertain ending as it is. After Dev posts the two transition tests, I’ll ask the group to listen once on headphones and once through a phone speaker. Thanks again, everyone; this is really helpful feedback.

input:
Mara: morning all, we’ve got a problem with saturday’s 9:30 group booking at willow bend. the family of six arrived early and two of the three canoes assigned to them are taking on water. nobody’s in danger, they’re still on the dock, but can someone help me sort out what we can offer?

Jo: checking the booking now. it’s under Patel, six people, three canoes, paid deposit of $90 on monday. they asked for the north loop and said two of the kids are first-time paddlers. i don’t see a phone number for the second adult, just Rina’s mobile.

Eli: i’m at the launch. canoe 14 has a steady drip near the rear seam, and canoe 22 has water coming in around the bow handle. i bailed both out, but they’re not suitable for a two-hour trip. the other canoe, 19, looks dry so far.

Mara: thanks for catching that before they left. did either one get checked after yesterday’s rental? the return sheet says 14 came back at 5:20, and there’s a note that the group had to pull it over a rocky patch near the inlet. no note on 22.

Ben: i can come down with the repair kit in about 25 minutes. i don’t want anyone using either canoe until i’ve looked at the seams and the handle mount. there are two spare tandems behind the shed, but i need to check the hulls and make sure the seats are in place.

Tess: the family asked whether they can still go out this morning or if they should reschedule. Rina said they drove an hour and packed lunch, so they’d rather not cancel. she also asked if the north loop is the only route where they can stay together.

Mara: tell them we’re checking the spare boats, and don’t promise a launch time yet. if the two spares are usable, we could keep the booking and explain the route options. can someone confirm whether the south cove route is open? the sign was down when i left last night.

Eli: south cove is open, but the water’s a little higher than usual after the rain. the route is still marked, and it avoids the narrow rocks by the inlet. it adds maybe 20 minutes if they take the inside bend. i wouldn’t call that a guaranteed beginner route, though.

Jo: i found the original booking note. Rina requested the north loop because her dad has a sore shoulder and wanted a shorter paddle. she didn’t say he can’t paddle, just that he may need breaks. the group selected the 9:30 start so they could be back by noon.

Tess: i spoke with Rina at the desk. she’s okay with waiting while we inspect the spares, but asked us to let her know before 10:15. she said her dad can sit in the middle and take breaks, and the kids have life jackets from home. we still need to fit them with ours before launch.

Ben: i checked the two spares. number 7 has no visible leaks and both seats are secure. number 11 has a cracked foot brace, but the hull and handles look fine. i’d use 7; i wouldn’t send 11 out until we replace the brace. the repair kit won’t tell us anything about that crack.

Mara: could we put one adult and two kids in 7, then the other adult and remaining child in 19? please check weight limits before we suggest that. also, if they use the south cove route, do we have a printed map we can hand over? i don’t want them relying on the faded post at the dock.

Eli: the posted limit for both 7 and 19 is 600 pounds, and the family’s booking form lists their combined weight as 685. we’d need to split them differently, and i don’t have individual weights. the printed south cove maps are in the blue box by the till; i checked yesterday and there were about ten left.

Jo: i can ask Rina for approximate weights, but should i mention why we need them? i don’t want that to sound strange at the counter. also, the booking includes two child-sized PFDs and four adult ones. one of the child PFDs is marked small, so we should check the fit rather than assume it works.

Tess: please explain that it’s for matching the group to the boats’ posted limits, not for changing their booking. i can help fit the PFDs. the family said one child is around 50 pounds and the other is about 70, but they weren’t sure about the adults’ weights. they’re waiting under the awning now.

Ben: i can inspect 14 and 22 when i finish checking 7. i haven’t diagnosed the leaks yet, so don’t tell the family those boats can be repaired today. if 19 and 7 aren’t a safe fit for all six, we may need another option from the shed or a later start.

Mara: can someone help me confirm what we can offer before 10:15? right now, 14 and 22 are out of use, 7 looks okay, and 19 hasn’t been load-checked. please check the remaining tandem, the group’s total weight against the boat limits, and whether a later north loop start is available. i’ll stay with Rina and explain that we’re still checking.

Eli: i can check the last tandem as soon as ben’s done with 7, and i’ll bring the map up from the till. i haven’t asked about a later start yet; the 11:00 group is booked for four boats, so we’d need to check the schedule before offering that. will post again once i have the boat details.

Jo: i’ll ask Rina for the adults’ approximate weights and confirm the PFD sizes now. i’ll keep it simple and say we’re checking the capacity of each boat before assigning seats. does anyone know if the north loop has enough room for a group to pause without blocking other renters? i can’t find that in the current guide.

input:
mara: quick question for the clock folks. i picked up a small oak mantel clock at the estate sale on Hawthorn St. last month. the seller said it came from her grandfather's shop, but there isn't a receipt or family note with it. the movement is stamped Ansonia, and the back door has a paper label that says "No. 14, 1907." does that date sound like a model date, or could it just be an inventory number?

theo: Ansonia used a lot of different labels, so i'd treat the paper date as a clue, not a firm date for the whole clock. Is there a date or patent line on the movement plate? Also, photos of the dial, hands and case corners might help narrow down the style. The company made loads of mantel clocks over a long stretch.

mara: i can get photos after work. the face is about 5 inches across, white enamel with black Roman numerals, and the minute hand has a little bend near the tip. case is roughly 11 inches tall. the seller said it ran when she was a kid, which doesn't tell us much, i know.

june: Check the bottom and the inside of the back panel too. Sometimes there’s a paper label tucked under the movement, or a penciled number on the wood. Don't scrape anything off to find it, though. Old paper can be fragile, and the label you found may be useful even if it isn't a date.

luis: On mine the movement plate has the maker name and patent dates, but they weren't the year mine was assembled. If yours has a gong coil, see if there’s a maker mark on that as well. I wouldn't use the gong or movement number by itself to date the case; parts can get changed.

mara: good point about the case and movement not necessarily matching. there's a brass gong at the back, one winding key in the drawer and two little holes on the dial, at 4 and 8. no key marked on the case. the back panel's loose at the top, so i'm trying not to handle it more than i need to.

eLI: For the winding holes, check that the key fits without forcing it. Some old keys are the wrong size, and a key can slip and scratch the dial. If it turns freely, that's one thing; if it catches or feels gritty, stop. A clock that's been sitting may need attention before anyone tries to run it.

theo: Also, don't assume the little bend in the minute hand is damage from use. It may have been bent at some point to clear something, or it could just be a bend. I'd avoid trying to straighten it while it's on the dial. A close photo from straight on would show whether the hands touch.

nina: If you're going to take the movement out, take a few pictures first and keep the screws in a labeled bag. But honestly, if you've never done one, I'd leave it in place for now. The wood case and the enamel dial can be cleaned very differently, and a general cleaner could do more harm than good.

mara: here's what i've noticed so far, in case it's useful: 1) the oak has a dark finish, worn lighter along the right front edge; 2) the glass door has a small chip at the bottom left; 3) the dial has a hairline mark from about 7 toward the center; 4) the pendulum is present, but i haven't tried hanging it.

june: That’s a good list. On the finish, I wouldn't put shellac, oil, or wax on it until you know what’s already there. Even a spot that looks dull can have old varnish on it. For the glass chip, just note where it is so you can tell if it changes; don't push on the edge to test it.

ravi: The label could be an inventory tag from the seller's grandfather's shop, like you said, but there's no way to know from that wording alone. A photo of the back of the movement and the label would be useful. If you post them, include one wider shot too so we can see how the movement sits in the case.

mara: thanks. i don't want to open the movement or clean it yet. i was mostly trying to figure out if 1907 is a reasonable clue, and whether i should look for anything specific before i take it to a repair person. i have a local horologist's name from the historical society, no appointment yet.

theo: I'd write down what came with it, including the key, and mention that you haven't wound it. Ask the horologist to check the movement and the case separately, and whether the hands are rubbing. You can also ask if they recognize the label, but I wouldn't treat their guess as proof of the exact year.

nina: One more thing: keep the clock upright and away from a radiator or sunny window while it's waiting. If you move it, support the case from underneath rather than lifting it by the top ornament. That finial can look sturdier than it is, especially if the glue has aged.

mara: got it. i'll photograph the label, movement plate, dial and case corners, and leave the key and pendulum alone for now. if anyone recognizes the "No. 14, 1907" label style from an Ansonia mantel clock, could you share what feature gives you confidence? even a likely range would help, as long as it's clear what's a guess.

input:
Mara: quick update from the clock room: we finished the first pass through the estate lot this morning. There are 18 clocks on the inventory sheet, including six mantel clocks, four wall clocks, three carriage clocks, and five longcase or bracket clocks. Nothing has been cleaned yet, so the notes reflect what we could see under the dust, not a final condition report.

Jon: The tall oak longcase is marked “J. H. Evans, Bristol” on the dial. Its brass weights and pendulum were wrapped separately in brown paper, and we found the winding key in the bottom drawer. The case has a split near the lower hinge, but the door still closes. I’ve photographed the maker’s mark and the split from both sides.

Leah: I checked the carriage clocks against the boxes. Two have their original leather cases, and one case has a cracked handle. The smallest clock has a silvered dial with Roman numerals and a retailer’s name from Bath; the lettering is partly worn. I haven’t tried winding any of them, since the springs and stops need a closer look first.

Mara: For the record, the blue transferware mantel clock is the one with the loose rear panel, not the clock in the green box. The green-box clock has a porcelain face with a small chip at seven o’clock. We’ve kept both boxes beside their clocks and added matching paper tags, so they won’t get separated during the room move.

Owen: I measured the walnut wall clock at 74 centimeters high, 31 wide, and 14 deep. The painted scene below the dial looks like a harbor, though the bottom edge is faded and I can’t make out the boat details. There’s a label inside the case reading “Regulator No. 42.” The pendulum is present; the key isn’t in the case or the drawer.

Priya: The brass bracket clock has a bell strike and a separate alarm hand. I noted both because the first inventory entry only said “brass clock.” The bell is wrapped in cloth beside the case, and the back door has two old screw holes near the latch. There’s no maker’s name visible on the movement from the angle we checked, so I left that field blank.

Mara: Here’s the room-by-room list for the next inventory pass:
1. East cabinet: six mantel clocks, two boxed parts trays, and the loose winding keys.
2. North wall: four wall clocks, including the walnut clock Owen measured.
3. Worktable: three carriage clocks and their two leather cases.
4. Alcove: five longcase or bracket clocks, with the oak case and brass bracket clock noted separately.
The count is still 18 clocks total. If anyone spots a mismatch, please flag the tag number rather than moving anything.

Jon: I found the tag for the small black mantel clock behind the ledger. It’s AR-116, and the entry says the case is ebonized wood. The finish has a few pale scuffs along the right side, but the feet are all present. There’s a handwritten card with it that reads, “From the front parlor, 1938.” We’ve kept the card in a sleeve with the tag.

Leah: Just adding a detail on the longcase clocks: the painted dial on the pine case has a moon phase disk, while the oak Evans clock has a plain seconds hand. The pine clock’s hood door is off its hinge and resting on a padded shelf. No one has attempted to rehang it. I added the shelf location to the condition notes so it’s easy to find.

Owen: I compared the wall-clock keys with the key ring in the office. One key fits the square arbor on the walnut clock, but I didn’t turn it. Two others are smaller and unmarked, and the remaining key has a tag reading “Workshop.” I’ve put them in a clear envelope marked for the clock room, rather than guessing which clock they belong to.

Mara: Thanks. The estate paperwork lists the clocks as coming from the house on Mill Lane, but it doesn’t give dates or purchase prices. A folder labeled “Repairs” contains two receipts from a shop in York, dated 1986 and 1991; both mention a mantel clock, but neither receipt has a model number. I’ve noted the folder reference without matching either receipt to a specific clock.

Priya: The glass on the square dial clock is convex and has a cloudy patch near the lower edge. The minute hand looks slightly bent in the photo, though it may just be the viewing angle. I took another picture straight on and left the first image in the folder too. The small brass finial was on the same shelf, but there’s no tag linking it to that clock yet.

Jon: The paper tags are holding up well, but the string on AR-109 is slipping against the case handle. I replaced the string and copied the number onto a fresh tag, then kept the old tag in the envelope with the notes. AR-109 is the mahogany mantel clock with the cream dial and black Arabic numerals. Its glass door opens from the left.

Leah: I’ve put the photo filenames into the shared sheet, including the close-ups of the worn Bath retailer’s name and the Bristol maker’s mark. The overview images show each clock beside its tag, and the detail images cover visible chips, splits, missing keys, or detached parts. There are no movement photographs yet. That can wait until the clocks are examined at the workbench.

Mara: That’s all for today. The room is locked, the two loose doors are on padded shelves, and the paperwork is back in the labeled folder. Tomorrow’s list is to verify the tags against the sheet, check the count once more, and record any parts we find in the drawers. We’re keeping the clocks where they are until the inventory pass is complete.

input:
hey folks, i'm a few weeks into learning ASL and keep getting stuck on fingerspelling when people go fast. in practice videos i can recognize letters one at a time, but when my friend spells a name or a street address, i lose track after the first few letters and then guess from context. that's not great, especially because i don't want to keep asking them to repeat everything 🙃

i've been trying to slow the videos down but then the hand movements look kind of different and i can't tell if i'm actually learning the shape or just memorizing the slowed version. i also mix up a couple letters that look similar to me, even though i know the orientation matters. i've watched the same beginner lesson a few times and i'm still not sure what to focus on.

could anyone recommend a good practice routine or a video/site that shows fingerspelling at a normal pace, with clear examples? if you have a trick for catching the transitions between letters, i'd love to hear it too. i'm not looking for a shortcut, just something more useful than replaying the same clip all evening. thanks! 🙏
output:
