our working plan for the North Quad Film Society's October program is to hold three Thursday screenings, on October 8, October 15, and October 22, 2026. This is still a proposed schedule, not a confirmed booking. The first film is City in Rain, with a running time of 84 minutes; the second is a group of shorts called Paper Moons, with a combined running time of 47 minutes; and the third is Last Stop, which runs for 91 minutes. We are asking the campus events office to reserve room B214 for each date. The room has 92 seats, and the film society would like to keep 12 of them available for students who arrive without registering. Doors are planned to open at 6:15 p.m., with each screening starting at 6:45 p.m. The start time should stay the same on all three dates, so students do not have to interpret a different schedule every week.

The draft schedule leaves room for a brief welcome before each screening, but it does not include a discussion afterward. For City in Rain, the film's distributor has quoted a runtime of 84 minutes, while the copy in the society's archive lists 83 minutes. The program coordinator is asking the distributor to verify which runtime should go on the public listing; until they reply, the 84-minute figure is the one in this draft. Paper Moons is made up of four shorts, and the 47-minute figure is the combined runtime supplied by the filmmaker. Last Stop has a 91-minute runtime on its licensing sheet. These times do not include introductions, and the society has not promised that every screening will finish at a particular time. The draft assumes that the welcome will take no more than five minutes, but it remains a planning estimate.

Room B214 is on the second floor of North Quad Hall. The building entrance on Cedar Walk has a ramp, and the events office directory lists an elevator near the east stairwell. We are asking the office to confirm that the elevator will be operating on all three evenings and that the room's aisle layout can accommodate a wheelchair user without blocking an exit. The society's access lead, Mina Patel, has also asked whether the room can be unlocked 30 minutes before doors open, so volunteers have time to check the projector and place the printed program sheets. If the room cannot be opened by 5:45 p.m., the access lead wants the society to move the equipment check to the student lounge rather than shorten the planned check. That is a request for the events office to consider, not a confirmed alternative booking.

The volunteer plan is organized around four roles, with the same assignments expected to apply on each date unless a volunteer reports a conflict.
1. The program coordinator will introduce the film and give the welcome. The coordinator is also responsible for checking that the announced running time matches the public listing once the distributor confirms the figure for City in Rain.
2. Two door volunteers will check student IDs and count attendance. They should record the number of people entering, not the number of seats left, and they should keep the 12 walk-in seats visible on the seating chart until the screening begins. The society has not decided whether any unused reserved seats will be released early.
3. One projection volunteer will test the playback file and sound level before doors open. For Paper Moons, that person should check all four shorts in their listed order and confirm that the combined file does not begin with the filmmaker's slate. The filmmaker has said, "the slate is for review, not for the audience," and the society is asking whether a version without the slate can be provided.
4. One access volunteer will keep the ramp-side aisle clear and bring the large-print program sheets to the entrance. The society has printed 18 large-print copies, based on requests received so far, but that number is not a cap on requests at the door.

The room request should be tracked under the filename below, because the campus events office asked the society to use one filename for the attendance estimate and equipment notes. The file is a working document, not a confirmed room reservation. The current estimate is 74 attendees on October 8, 68 on October 15, and 80 on October 22. Each number is an estimate for that date, not a count of registrations. The equipment notes ask for one HDMI cable, two handheld microphones, and a standing lamp at the entrance. The projection volunteer has already checked that the society owns one HDMI adapter, but has not checked whether it works with the room's projector.

delivery-summary.tsv

For publicity, the society is preparing one digital poster and 60 printed copies for the student center and the library noticeboard. The poster draft includes all three dates, the 6:45 p.m. start time, and a note that admission is free for currently enrolled students. The society is asking the communications desk to review the poster's use of the college wordmark before printing. The wordmark is not yet cleared for this use. The student center allows posters on the north display panel, while the library noticeboard requires approval from its desk staff; volunteers should not assume that permission for one location covers the other. The society would like to post the digital version on September 21, if the wordmark review is complete by then. If the review is still pending on September 21, the coordinator wants to hold the digital post and use a text-only listing in the weekly bulletin instead. The printed copies are to wait until the wordmark question is resolved, even if that means they are not available for the first week of publicity.

The draft budget lists $180 for the three screening licenses, $36 for printing, and $24 for refreshments. The $180 license figure is the total quoted amount, not a per-film amount; it covers the three listed program dates, subject to the distributor's final confirmation of the City in Rain runtime. The printing figure covers 60 standard copies and 18 large-print copies, and the society has asked the campus print desk whether both sizes can be charged to the same order. The refreshments amount is a ceiling for bottled water and packaged snacks, not an instruction to spend the full amount. The treasurer has asked the student activities office whether the society may use its remaining $90 from the fall events allocation toward these costs. That balance is recorded in the society's spreadsheet, but the office has not confirmed that it is available for this program. Until there is a reply, the $90 should remain a possible contribution rather than being subtracted from the total budget request.

The society is also checking whether a short introduction by filmmaker Jo Alvarez is possible for the October 15 program. Alvarez's assistant said, "Jo may be in town that week, but we cannot confirm a visit yet." The coordinator is asking the assistant to confirm availability by September 28. No travel or appearance payment is included in the current budget, and the society has not asked Alvarez to attend remotely. If the assistant confirms a visit, the coordinator wants to ask the events office whether the room can be entered 15 minutes earlier that evening; if there is no confirmation by September 28, the screening should continue with the standard welcome by the program coordinator. The draft should therefore leave Alvarez's name out of the public poster for now, while keeping the possible introduction in the internal schedule notes.

The remaining planning questions are the distributor's confirmed runtime for City in Rain, the operation of the elevator, the room's early-unlock time, the wordmark review, and whether the $90 allocation can be used. Mina Patel is following up with the events office about access and room opening, while the program coordinator is handling the distributor and publicity questions. The treasurer will contact the student activities office about the allocation. The society wants those separate replies recorded against the relevant dates and costs, rather than treating any pending item as settled. The October 8 attendance estimate of 74 should remain in the working file until registration opens, and the door volunteers will use the actual entry count on the evening itself. The room booking, equipment request, and public listing are still being prepared from this draft, with the October dates and shared 6:45 p.m. start time as the basis for the requests.

transfer.allow_resume
I found it in the advanced section, but I'm not sure whether it applies to queued files or only a file that's already moving. Please explain that distinction without changing any other setting. The first batch has 24 folders, and each folder has 18 files; that's 24 folders, not 24 files total. Ich beschreibe den Fahrkartentausch, den ich am Dienstag am Schalter im Leipziger Hauptbahnhof angefragt habe. Ich heiße Jana Keller und habe die ursprüngliche Fahrkarte online für meinen Vater Rolf Keller gebucht. Es ist seine Fahrkarte, nicht meine, auch wenn die Buchung über mein Kundenkonto lief. Sie gilt für eine einfache Fahrt von Leipzig nach Erfurt am 18. Mai um 17:42 Uhr. Mein Vater wollte an dem Tag nach Erfurt zurückfahren, nachdem er mich in Leipzig besucht hatte. Bei der Buchung hatte ich die Angaben mit ihm am Telefon durchgesprochen und den Termin so eingetragen, wie er ihn mir genannt hatte.

Am Montagabend rief mein Vater wieder an. Der Termin, wegen dem er am Samstagvormittag in Erfurt sein muss, wurde nach seiner Aussage nach vorne gelegt, und er möchte deshalb schon am 19. Mai früher dort ankommen. Er bat mich, nach einer anderen Verbindung zu schauen und für ihn den Tausch anzufragen. Er selbst hat die neue Wunschzeit genannt: am 19. Mai möglichst um 15:35 Uhr. Ich habe ihm gesagt, dass ich am Schalter zuerst nach den Möglichkeiten und den Kosten frage und noch nicht versprechen kann, dass genau diese Verbindung klappt. Am Dienstag nahm ich deshalb die ausgedruckte Fahrkarte und die Buchungsnummer mit zum Bahnhof.

Am Schalter war Herr Aydin zuständig. Ich erklärte ihm, dass ich die Anfrage für die Fahrkarte meines Vaters stelle, und dass die geänderte Fahrkarte, falls ein Tausch zustande kommt, an meine E-Mail-Adresse gehen soll. Das ist jana.keller@example.de. Mein Vater verwendet seine E-Mail-Adresse nur selten und hatte mich ausdrücklich gebeten, die Nachricht für ihn zu empfangen. Ich bat Herrn Aydin um einen Tausch vom 18. auf den 19. Mai, nach Möglichkeit für die Abfahrt um 15:35 Uhr. Er schaute die Buchung auf seinem Bildschirm nach und verglich dabei Namen, Strecke, Datum und Zugnummer.

Herr Aydin sagte, dass die Fahrkarte ein Sparpreis ist. Laut seiner Auskunft kann sie vor der Abfahrt des gebuchten Zuges geändert werden, wenn der Fahrpreis für die neue Verbindung bezahlt wird; zusätzlich fällt eine Bearbeitungsgebühr von 19 Euro an. Er sagte nicht, dass der Tausch bereits ausgeführt sei, sondern erklärte mir erst die verfügbaren Möglichkeiten. Für den Zug um 15:35 Uhr am 19. Mai konnte er im Moment keinen freien Platz sehen. Er fand aber einen Zug um 16:10 Uhr, für den die Buchung grundsätzlich möglich sei. Der Gesamtpreis würde sich dabei um 12 Euro erhöhen, zusätzlich zu der genannten Gebühr.

Ich fragte, ob die Verbindung um 15:35 Uhr später noch einmal geprüft werden könne, weil meinem Vater diese Zeit besser passt. Herr Aydin erklärte, dass er die Verfügbarkeit am Schalter nicht für den ganzen Tag reservieren könne. Er bot stattdessen an, die Möglichkeit für den Zug um 16:10 Uhr bis Mittwoch um 12 Uhr offen zu halten. Wenn ich bis dahin bestätige und die Mehrkosten samt Gebühr bezahle, kann er den Tausch auf diese Verbindung bearbeiten. Wenn ich bis Mittwochmittag nicht bestätige, fällt diese Vormerkung weg. Das Angebot bezieht sich nur auf den Zug um 16:10 Uhr; es ist keine Zusage, dass am Mittwoch ein Platz im Zug um 15:35 Uhr frei wird.

Ich schrieb die Auskunft während des Gesprächs in mein Notizbuch, damit ich meinem Vater die Beträge und die Frist richtig nennen kann. Herr Aydin gab mir außerdem einen kleinen Ausdruck mit der bisherigen Buchung und den Angaben zum möglichen neuen Zug. Auf dem Ausdruck steht weiterhin das Datum 18. Mai, weil die Änderung noch nicht vorgenommen wurde. Die ursprüngliche Fahrkarte hatte ich nach dem Gespräch wieder in die Mappe gelegt. Sie trägt den Namen Rolf Keller und die Sitzplatzangabe Wagen 6, Platz 42 am Fenster. Herr Aydin sagte, bei einem Tausch könnten Sitzplatzangaben abweichen; über einen Fensterplatz könne er für die neue Verbindung im Augenblick nichts bestätigen.

Für meinen Vater habe ich die wichtigen Punkte in drei Teile sortiert:
1. Die bestehende Fahrkarte gilt für Rolf Keller, Leipzig nach Erfurt, am 18. Mai um 17:42 Uhr. Die Anfrage betrifft einen Tausch auf den 19. Mai, nicht eine zweite Fahrkarte und nicht eine Fahrt für mich.
2. Die von meinem Vater gewünschte Abfahrt ist 15:35 Uhr. Herr Aydin konnte dafür derzeit keinen freien Platz sehen. Als andere Möglichkeit nannte er 16:10 Uhr; der Preis läge 12 Euro höher, und die Bearbeitungsgebühr beträgt laut seiner Auskunft 19 Euro.
3. Nur die Möglichkeit für 16:10 Uhr ist bis Mittwoch, 12 Uhr, vorgemerkt. Damit der Tausch auf dieser Verbindung bearbeitet werden kann, muss ich bis dahin bestätigen und die Mehrkosten samt Gebühr bezahlen. Die Vormerkung gilt nicht als schon erfolgter Tausch.

Am Dienstagabend rief ich meinen Vater an und las ihm diese Punkte vor. Er bestätigte, dass die Fahrkarte auf seinen Namen ausgestellt ist und dass ich den Tausch für ihn anfragen sollte. Bei der Uhrzeit wollte er noch überlegen, weil er lieber um 15:35 Uhr fahren würde, aber auch wissen möchte, ob die Verbindung um 16:10 Uhr für ihn noch passt. Ich sagte ihm, dass ich ihm keine Verfügbarkeit für 15:35 Uhr versprechen kann und dass die Vormerkung für 16:10 Uhr nur bis Mittwochmittag gilt. Er bat mich, ihm den Ausdruck abzufotografieren und die Nachricht von der Bahn an meine E-Mail-Adresse schicken zu lassen, falls es später zu einem Tausch kommt. Eine Bestätigung für die Änderung habe ich ihm am Dienstag nicht gegeben.

Der Ausdruck liegt jetzt zusammen mit der ursprünglichen Fahrkarte in meiner Mappe, und ich habe die Frist Mittwoch um 12 Uhr in meinem Kalender eingetragen. Falls mein Vater bis dahin die Verbindung um 16:10 Uhr bestätigt und ich die genannten Beträge bezahle, kann Herr Aydin den Tausch bearbeiten und die neue Fahrkarte an jana.keller@example.de schicken. Falls er sich dagegen nicht rechtzeitig festlegt, bleibt es bei der bestehenden Fahrkarte für den 18. Mai um 17:42 Uhr; die vorgemerkte Möglichkeit für den Zug um 16:10 Uhr wäre dann nicht mehr offen. Über einen freien Platz um 15:35 Uhr liegt weiterhin keine Auskunft vor.

Ich sagte ihm, dass ich am Schalter zunächst nach den Möglichkeiten und Kosten fragen würde. Ob genau diese Verbindung klappt, konnte ich ihm noch nicht versprechen. Am Dienstag nahm ich deshalb die ausgedruckte Fahrkarte und die Buchungsnummer mit zum Bahnhof.

Herr Aydin war am Schalter zuständig. Ich erklärte ihm, dass ich den Tausch für die Fahrkarte meines Vaters anfrage. Falls es zu einem Tausch kommt, soll die geänderte Fahrkarte an meine E-Mail-Adresse jana.keller@example.de geschickt werden. Mein Vater verwendet seine E-Mail-Adresse nur selten und hatte mich ausdrücklich gebeten, die Nachricht für ihn zu empfangen. Ich bat Herrn Aydin, die Fahrt vom 18. auf den 19. Mai zu tauschen, möglichst auf die Abfahrt um 15:35 Uhr. Er rief die Buchung am Bildschirm auf und verglich dabei Name, Strecke, Datum und Zugnummer.

Herr Aydin sagte, dass es sich um eine Sparpreis-Fahrkarte handelt. Seiner Auskunft nach kann sie vor der Abfahrt des gebuchten Zuges geändert werden, sofern der Fahrpreis für die neue Verbindung bezahlt wird. Zusätzlich fällt eine Bearbeitungsgebühr von 19 Euro an. Er führte den Tausch nicht aus, sondern erklärte mir zunächst die verfügbaren Möglichkeiten. Für den Zug am 19. Mai um 15:35 Uhr konnte er derzeit keinen freien Platz sehen. Er fand jedoch einen Zug um 16:10 Uhr, für den eine Buchung grundsätzlich möglich wäre. Der Gesamtpreis wäre dabei um 12 Euro höher, zusätzlich zur genannten Gebühr.

Ich fragte, ob er die Verbindung um 15:35 Uhr später noch einmal prüfen könne, da diese Zeit meinem Vater besser passt. Herr Aydin erklärte, dass er die Verfügbarkeit am Schalter nicht für den ganzen Tag reservieren kann. Stattdessen bot er an, die Möglichkeit für den Zug um 16:10 Uhr bis Mittwoch um 12 Uhr vorzumerken. Wenn ich bis dahin bestätige und die Mehrkosten samt Gebühr bezahle, kann er den Tausch auf diese Verbindung bearbeiten. Bestätige ich nicht bis Mittwochmittag, verfällt die Vormerkung. Das Angebot gilt nur für den Zug um 16:10 Uhr; es ist keine Zusage, dass am Mittwoch ein Platz für den Zug um 15:35 Uhr frei sein wird.

Während des Gesprächs schrieb ich die Auskunft in mein Notizbuch, damit ich meinem Vater die Beträge und die Frist richtig nennen kann. Herr Aydin gab mir außerdem einen kleinen Ausdruck mit der bisherigen Buchung und den Angaben zum möglichen neuen Zug. Darauf steht weiterhin der 18. Mai, weil die Änderung noch nicht vorgenommen wurde. Nach dem Gespräch legte ich die ursprüngliche Fahrkarte wieder in meine Mappe. Sie trägt den Namen Rolf Keller und die Sitzplatzangabe Wagen 6, Platz 42 am Fenster. Herr Aydin sagte, dass die Sitzplatzangaben bei einem Tausch abweichen können. Ob es auf der neuen Verbindung einen Fensterplatz gibt, könne er derzeit nicht bestätigen.

Für meinen Vater habe ich die wichtigsten Punkte in drei Teile gegliedert:
1. Die bestehende Fahrkarte gilt für Rolf Keller, von Leipzig nach Erfurt, am 18. Mai um 17:42 Uhr. Angefragt ist ein Tausch auf den 19. Mai, keine zweite Fahrkarte und keine Fahrt für mich.
2. Mein Vater wünscht eine Abfahrt um 15:35 Uhr. Herr Aydin konnte dafür derzeit keinen freien Platz sehen. Als Alternative nannte er 16:10 Uhr. Der Preis wäre 12 Euro höher; dazu kommt die Bearbeitungsgebühr von 19 Euro.
3. Nur die Möglichkeit für 16:10 Uhr ist bis Mittwoch um 12 Uhr vorgemerkt. Damit der Tausch auf dieser Verbindung bearbeitet werden kann, muss ich bis dahin bestätigen und die Mehrkosten samt Gebühr bezahlen. Die Vormerkung bedeutet nicht, dass der Tausch bereits erfolgt ist.

Am Dienstagabend rief ich meinen Vater an und las ihm diese Punkte vor. Er bestätigte, dass die Fahrkarte auf seinen Namen ausgestellt ist und dass ich den Tausch für ihn anfragen sollte. Bei der Uhrzeit wollte er noch überlegen: Er würde lieber um 15:35 Uhr fahren, möchte aber auch prüfen, ob 16:10 Uhr für ihn passt. please include the query below as supplied reference material in the prompt, intact. it is the query the analyst plans to use for a received-units-by-depot check. don't rewrite its filter, and don't imply that it has already been run or that its results are attached. SELECT depot_id, SUM(units) AS received_units
FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'received' AND units > 9
GROUP BY depot_id;

For dates with no matching received rows, say what the records show and leave the reason open. If the records don't let the analyst establish something, say that briefly instead of filling the gap.

If a refreshed export is not available, leave the coverage question unresolved; don't substitute an assumed cutoff or claim the last evening had no deliveries. Keep that condition in the prompt, since it changes what the analyst can say about the monthly total. The final summary should make no claim about deliveries outside North Quay or dates outside April, and it should not turn the query into a result. the subtitle file for the Harbor Glass concert at Bellwether Hall on June 14 is being handled by me, Inez, the production coordinator. I started the file from the band's approved lyric sheet, which reached us on May 28, and the running order that venue manager Tomas sent the same afternoon. It has 19 songs and two short spoken introductions, and the current version is called harbor_glass_bellwether_0614_v3.srt. We are using English subtitles only. I am keeping the title cards out of this file because the venue loads those separately, and the opening card already has a separate delivery slot.

Jo is the subtitle editor, and Jo made the first timing pass after the June 2 rehearsal recording arrived. That recording was 42 minutes long and had the band's lead singer, Nia Vale, speaking between songs. Jo matched the lyrics against the approved sheet, then adjusted the spoken sections by listening to the recording. Jo told me, “I left the audience shouts alone unless they covered a lyric.” That means the file includes the shouted “one more song” before the encore, but it does not include every cheer heard under the final chorus. The rehearsal recording is not the concert mix, so I told Jo not to use it to set the final sound cue points.

I sent the current subtitle file to Leena, the venue projectionist, and asked her to check whether the stage screen will be full-width or whether the two narrow side panels will also be used. I need Leena to answer before Jo settles the line breaks, because the smaller panels allow fewer characters per line. Leena has not confirmed the arrangement yet. If she confirms that only the full-width screen will be used, Jo can keep the longer two-line breaks already in v3. If Leena says the side panels are in use, Jo will need to make a second layout with shorter lines; that is a proposal for the next pass, not work that has happened already. I asked Leena to reply by June 10, since Jo has a separate captioning job on June 11 and 12.

There are a few details in the lyric sheet that need to stay exactly as written. The song “Glass Harbor” is the third song, even though the title sounds like the venue name, and its lyric includes the phrase “we keep the light on.” In “Northbound,” Nia sings “I found my way home” twice, with a short instrumental break between the two lines. The lyric sheet has both lines, but Jo has timed them as separate subtitle cues to match the performance. I also checked the names in the spoken introduction: Nia introduces the touring drummer, Ellis Park, and thanks local opener June Arcade. Ellis uses they/them pronouns in the band's notes. Jo put the names on their own lines because the introduction is quick, and I asked Jo not to shorten June Arcade to “June,” which could sound like a date in the file review notes.

1. The file uses a 24-frame-per-second time base, matching the playback package that venue technician Ravi gave me. Jo checked the first cue against the rehearsal recording at 00:01:12, and I checked the last lyric cue against the end of the encore. The file has no subtitle during the two-second black screen before the first song. Ravi said the playback package accepts SRT files, but he has not tested this particular version on the house system.
2. The house screen is normally set to white text with a thin dark outline. Leena told me that the font size is controlled in the projection system, not in the subtitle file, so Jo did not add styling tags. The band's lighting plan includes a bright amber wash during “Northbound,” which made two lines hard to read on the rehearsal monitor. Jo moved those cues a little earlier where the vocal allowed it, but did not change the words or remove either line. The rehearsal monitor is smaller than the hall screen, and we do not know yet whether the side panels will be active.
3. I asked Ravi to check the file's final cue and the playback start point during the technical check on June 13. That is a request, not a report that he has tested them. If the venue asks for a fresh export after Jo adjusts the layout, I will send Ravi the new file name and ask him to replace v3 in the playback folder. Until Leena replies, I have not asked Jo to export a second layout, and Ravi still has only the current version.
4. The band's manager, Sal, requested a copy for review before the show, and I told Sal I would send the next checked version after the screen layout is known. Sal did not ask to approve the lyrics, which came from the band-approved sheet; Sal asked to review the timing and spelling of the names. I have kept the rehearsal recording in the production drive, separate from the subtitle folder, because it includes private comments before the first song. Jo has access to the subtitle folder but not to that separate recording folder, so I sent Jo the rehearsal audio through the production review link instead.

I am keeping the review notes beside the file rather than inside it, so they do not appear as audience subtitles. My latest note says that Jo should recheck the spoken introduction after the line breaks are set, because the names and thanks happen in quick succession. Jo has not made that final check yet. The next file I send to Sal will still be identified as a review copy, and I will include the version name and the screen arrangement Leena confirms. If Leena has not replied by June 10, I will tell Jo that the layout question is still open rather than treating the full-width screen as confirmed. The subtitle folder currently contains v3, the approved lyric sheet, and the review notes; it does not contain a second layout or a tested playback export.

hey, can you turn this into a clear prompt for explaining and reviewing the sql below? i'm helping the morning team at North Quay depot understand a delivery summary that someone copied into a draft handover note. The note is meant to help the shift lead compare incoming volume across depots, but the only thing i have to work from is this query. Please base the explanation and review on the snippet itself, not on assumptions about our database, dashboard, or warehouse process. don't run it or pretend we have results; i need a request that asks someone to explain what the code says and what it leaves open.

The handover is being assembled for a Monday meeting, and the team has asked whether the query is intended to describe a particular week. I can't see a date field or a date condition in the code, so please make that a point to check rather than quietly treating it as a weekly total. A driver called Lina said, “I thought received units meant everything unloaded at the gate.” The shift lead, Omar, replied, “Maybe, but I want to know what this query actually counts before we put that in the note.” Those are their comments, not definitions of the fields. Keep the explanation grounded in the code and don't choose between their interpretations unless the snippet supports it.

Here is the complete snippet as it was sent to me. It has four lines, and the last line matters because it shows how the rows are grouped. Please keep the supplied lines together in the prompt, so the person reviewing it can see the entire query rather than being told to find it elsewhere.

SELECT depot_id, SUM(units) AS received_units
FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'received' AND units > 42
GROUP BY depot_id;

I am asking for an explanation that a depot shift lead can follow without assuming they already know SQL. Cover what table the query names, which fields appear in its output, what the SUM is doing, and what the alias received_units labels. Explain the filter carefully: there are two conditions joined in the WHERE clause, and both must be true for a row to be included. In particular, help the reviewer distinguish the status check from the numeric units check. Don't turn this into a claim about total units from every delivery, because the query has a threshold and a status filter. The team is trying to read the code accurately, not to make a general statement about depot activity.

Please also review the sequence of operations in ordinary language, especially how rows that pass the filter are collected by depot_id and how the displayed sum relates to that grouping. If the code does not tell us what a depot identifier means, whether units are cases or individual items, or what period the table covers, say those details are not established here. We use printed depot labels on the loading board, but I don't know whether those labels correspond exactly to depot_id, so don't equate them. No schema, sample records, or report definition was provided with the snippet. Keep those gaps separate from things the query does state.

For the review, call out questions that follow directly from the text of the query rather than proposing a replacement. For example, ask whether leaving out rows with units of 42 or less is intended, and whether the status spelling in the filter matches the values used in the deliveries table; the code alone doesn't confirm either business choice. You can mention that the condition is strictly greater than 42, not greater than or equal to 42. Don't claim that the chosen threshold is wrong or right. If the explanation cannot establish what the business team means by received, mark that as something to confirm instead of supplying a definition.

A small test section would be useful, but it should describe cases to check, not provide fabricated output. Include a row whose status is received and whose units are above 42, a row with another status, and a received row at exactly 42. Also ask what happens when qualifying rows share a depot_id, since that is relevant to the grouping and sum. Avoid assigning example depots, counts, or totals that are not in the code. If the reviewer cannot determine expected results without table contents, say so; the request is to identify useful checks, not to invent records or run the query.

There is a second note from the coordinator, Priya: “Please keep the handover plain enough to read aloud, but don't hide the filter.” That should shape the requested explanation without changing its meaning. reader.prefer_local

please revise our bakery's order form so customers can use it for celebration cakes, pastry trays, and weekday bread orders without needing a separate sheet for each kind. right now, the form asks for a name and phone number, but it doesn't give people a clear place to say what they want or when they need it. we take orders at the counter and by phone, and staff copy phone orders onto the same form. keep the form useful for both ways of ordering, and make the fields clear enough that someone can check the order later without relying on memory.

At the top, include the customer's name, best phone number, and email address, with a note that email is optional. Add the date the order is placed, the requested pickup date, and a pickup time. We are open Tuesday through Sunday, from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. for pickups. A customer should be able to enter a preferred time, but the form should not make it sound like that time is already confirmed. Leave a staff-only space to write the confirmed pickup time after checking the calendar. There should also be a place for the staff member who took the order to put their initials.

For the order itself, provide space for the product name, quantity, size or serving count, and price. Cake orders need a line for flavor, filling, frosting, and a short description of decoration. We offer 6-inch, 8-inch, and 10-inch round cakes, as well as quarter-sheet and half-sheet cakes. The form can list those choices, but it should leave room for a different size to be requested. If a customer asks for writing on a cake, provide a box for the exact wording, and label it so staff know to copy the customer's wording rather than correct it. If no writing is requested, leave that box blank rather than filling it with a dash.

The form also needs to distinguish between requests we can plan for and things that are confirmed. A customer can request a color or a particular style, but that doesn't mean we have promised it. Please include a notes field for those requests and a separate staff field for whether the bakery can accommodate them. One customer recently said, "simple flowers, nothing too tall," and another asked for a blue cake but said, "any shade is fine." Those are useful examples of how customers may describe decoration, but don't print the examples on the form. Keep the fields general enough for other requests too.

1. Put allergy information in a prominent section, separate from decoration notes. Ask the customer to list any allergy or dietary concern, and include a checkbox for "No allergy or dietary concerns reported." If a concern is listed, staff should not treat the checkbox as checked. The form should direct staff to review the concern with the baker before confirming the order. We use shared equipment, so the form must not imply that we can guarantee an allergen-free product. For a phone order, staff should write the customer's words as closely as possible and read them back before ending the call.

2. Include a payment section that records the quoted total, deposit received, remaining balance, and payment method. We accept cash and card in the shop, and customers may pay the full amount when ordering or pay a deposit. A deposit is $10 for orders under $50 and 25 percent of the quoted total for orders of $50 or more. If the order total changes after the customer approves a change, staff should update the quoted total and remaining balance; otherwise, they should leave those amounts as originally recorded. Please give staff a place to note the date a deposit was received, since it may not be the same as the date the form was first filled out.

Some orders change after they are placed, especially decoration details or the number of items in a pastry tray. Include a change log with the date, the requested change, the staff member who discussed it, and whether the customer approved any change in price. Do not make the form suggest that a requested change is accepted just because it has been written down. If a change affects the price, staff should tell the customer the revised amount and record whether the customer approved it. If the customer does not approve the revised price, keep the original order details and mark the change as not approved, rather than replacing the original details.

For timing, we need to know whether an order is routine or needs a short lead time. Customers should be asked to submit cake orders at least 48 hours before pickup and pastry tray orders at least 24 hours before pickup. Bread orders can be placed by 2 p.m. on the day before pickup. If an order arrives later than the relevant cutoff, staff should check with the baker before saying it can be made; if the baker cannot take it, staff should record that it was not accepted, rather than entering it as a confirmed order. This matters because the printed pickup date alone could otherwise look like a promise. Include a space to record the baker's response and the time staff checked.

Please make the form workable on paper and as a fillable digital file. On paper, there should be enough writing room for an order with more than one product, and staff should be able to attach a second page without losing the customer's name or pickup date. For the digital version, use checkboxes only where more than one choice is genuinely available, and keep the fields for written descriptions open for typing. We sometimes receive phone orders while the counter is busy, so avoid tiny labels or a layout that requires staff to jump between distant sections to find the pickup details and payment information.

At the bottom, add a space for the customer to confirm the order details and a separate staff check that the pickup date and time were reviewed against the calendar. Do not label the customer's confirmation as proof that the bakery has accepted a late order; acceptance still depends on the baker's response when a cutoff has passed. Include a final space for staff to note any follow-up that is still needed, such as calling the customer back about a decoration request. Leave that space open rather than pre-filling it with a standard message, since not every order needs follow-up.

our shared bicycle shed sits behind the west entrance of Alder Court, between the laundry room and the low brick wall. It was put in place in 2019, and the residents' committee has kept a paper key register since then. The shed has twelve marked spaces, although there are usually more than twelve bicycles in it by Friday evening. The committee says the spaces are for residents, not visitors, but it has not made a separate rule about short visits. I use the shed most days, and I find the narrow entrance slightly awkward when I have panniers on both sides of my bike.

The roof is corrugated plastic, and its front edge is lower than the back edge, so rain runs toward the drain along the wall. One roof panel became loose during a windy night in March. Mara from apartment 2B tied it down temporarily with cord, and the committee arranged a repair the following week. The repaired panel is still a different shade from the others. On sunny afternoons the roof makes the shed bright enough to see the number tags, but the rear corner stays dim. There is one motion-sensor light there, and it comes on after a short delay. Residents have mentioned the delay a few times, though nobody has asked for the light to be replaced.

The entrance latch catches if the door is pulled shut too quickly. People sometimes leave it open while they move a bicycle through, which makes the latch issue less noticeable but leaves the doorway exposed to the rain. The committee posted a small sign saying, “Please pull the door until it clicks.” That has helped a little, especially when children are bringing in smaller bikes. The sign is attached with two screws, one of which is beginning to loosen. If the door does not latch after the next adjustment, the committee has said it will ask the caretaker to look at the frame as well. That condition matters because the caretaker is not being asked to work on the frame yet.

There are two floor pumps on the shelf beside the entrance. The blue pump belongs to the shed, and the silver one was left there by a resident who moved out last autumn. The blue pump has a pressure gauge that is hard to read, while the silver one has no gauge. I usually check tire pressure at home, so this is not a large problem for me, but other residents have borrowed the pumps before weekend rides. A handwritten note on the shelf says, “Put the pump back when you are finished.” It is clear enough, although the paper curls at the corners and is occasionally covered by gloves or a helmet.

1. Space and access: the painted numbers run from 1 to 12, with spaces 1 and 2 nearest the entrance. Space 12 is next to the rear wall, where a pipe narrows the available room. A long cargo bike can fit there only if its front wheel is turned toward the center aisle. The committee has not assigned spaces to particular apartments, and residents choose an open one when they arrive. There is no written limit on how long a bicycle may be left in the shed. At the last residents' meeting, someone asked whether an unused bike could be moved after a month, but the minutes record that the committee would discuss it later.

The floor is concrete, with a shallow channel leading to a drain near the back. Leaves and small bits of gravel collect in the channel after wet weather. Theo in 4A sweeps it out every couple of weeks, although he says he does it when he notices it rather than on a schedule. A small patch beside the drain is darker than the rest of the floor. It was already there when I moved into Alder Court, and I do not know what caused it. The caretaker looked at it last summer and said, “It seems dry at the moment.” No repair was arranged, and the patch has not visibly changed since then.

The committee keeps a box of spare reflectors, two cable ties, and a few paper labels in a cupboard inside the shed. The cupboard key is kept with the main shed key in the laundry-room office. To borrow something from the box, a resident is meant to write their apartment number in the register, but people do not always remember. Last month, someone left a note saying that a red rear reflector was missing. The committee added two reflectors to the box the next day, but it is not known whether either one was the original reflector. There are also three abandoned-looking locks on the shelf; nobody has identified their owners, so they have not been removed.

The lighting and access were discussed at the committee's February meeting. A resident in 6C said, “I can see the entrance, but not the back wheel when I am locking up.” Another resident said the sensor had worked fine for them. The minutes describe both comments, and say the committee will check the light when the electrician next visits the building. They do not give a date for that visit. The committee also agreed to replace the curling pump note with a plastic sleeve, but only if a spare sleeve can be found in the building office. If there is no spare sleeve, the note will stay as it is for now. I think the light is probably adequate for ordinary use, though the rear corner is harder to see on cloudy evenings.

Residents generally make room for one another, but the aisle can become crowded when several people arrive at the same time. Last Thursday, two bikes were being moved through the doorway while another resident was trying to turn a cargo bike near space 12. Everyone waited a moment, and the bikes went in without anyone needing to take one back outside. A small basket on the shelf holds discarded bell parts and reflectors, not items for general use. The committee has not decided what to do with the three locks or whether to introduce assigned spaces. For now, the numbered spaces remain open for residents to use, and the register and cupboard key are kept in the laundry-room office.

The propagation greenhouse at Alder Creek Farm uses a written watering rota to keep work consistent across its three growing bays. Bay A holds seed trays and young plugs, Bay B contains herbs and leafy crops, and Bay C is reserved for tomatoes, peppers, and other fruiting plants. The rota is posted beside the wash sink and copied to a waterproof clipboard near the main entrance. It identifies the person responsible for each shift, the expected checks, and the time at which any unfinished work must be handed over. The system is designed for a small team whose schedules overlap only briefly, so each entry needs to be clear enough for someone who did not see the previous shift.

Watering is planned around the condition of the plants rather than a fixed daily quantity. Staff check the surface and weight of representative pots, inspect the drainage trays, and compare their observations with the moisture notes recorded the day before. A dry-looking surface alone does not establish that a root ball needs water, particularly in the larger containers in Bay C. Conversely, seed trays in Bay A can dry quickly near the warm-air outlet, even when the surrounding benches feel cool. The person on duty records whether watering was needed, which bench was checked, and any unusual change in leaf color or growth. This gives the next shift a useful history without turning routine observations into diagnoses.

The regular rota runs from Monday through Saturday, with a shorter inspection on Sunday. The opening shift begins at 7:30 a.m. and checks the hose connections, water temperature, and the level in the rainwater tank before using the watering wand. The afternoon shift starts at 1:00 p.m. and reviews the morning notes before deciding whether a second check is necessary. Staff avoid watering leaves late in the day because damp foliage can remain wet overnight. When a scheduled check is postponed by deliveries or maintenance, the person responsible writes the revised time on the clipboard rather than leaving the next person to guess whether the task was completed.

1. **Bay A — propagation:** Check the moisture of the seed trays and plug cells at the front, center, and warm-air end of each bench. Use the narrow-spout can for small cells and apply water slowly, allowing it to soak in rather than run across the tray. If a tray is already evenly moist, record the check and do not water it again just to match another tray. Move any standing water from beneath the cells after the final check.
2. **Bay B — herbs and leafy crops:** Inspect one container from each bench and check the bed edges as well as the center. Water at soil level, taking care not to wash compost onto the walkway. The basil bench dries faster than the parsley bench on sunny days, but its condition still needs to be checked before watering. Mark any blocked drainage hole for the maintenance list.
3. **Bay C — fruiting plants:** Check the soil beside the stems without disturbing roots, and look for water in the saucers. Use the marked jug to keep the amount consistent when a pot requires water. Do not treat a curled leaf by itself as proof that a plant is dry; compare the soil and the latest temperature note first. Record any pot that remains unusually light after watering so it can be inspected again.
4. **Shared equipment:** Rinse the wand and cans after use, return them to their labeled hooks, and close the tank valve. If the hose coupling leaks, place the red tag on it and notify the shift lead before the next watering round. Do not leave a hose stretched across the central aisle, even when another person is expected to use it shortly afterward.

The rota includes a weather and temperature check because greenhouse conditions can change quickly when cloud cover shifts or a vent is left open. The thermometer beside Bay B is read at the start of both shifts, and the reading is written beside the date rather than in a separate notebook. If the overnight forecast is below 10°C, the closing shift checks that the vent levers are secured and tells the morning staff to assess the pots before opening the vents. This condition matters to the watering decision: cold, wet compost can remain saturated for longer, so the morning worker must rely on the pot checks and not assume that the usual early watering is appropriate. If the thermometer reading differs sharply from the forecast, the shift lead is informed and the discrepancy is recorded.

Several practical details help the rota work during busy periods. The rainwater tank usually supplies the greenhouse, while the mains tap is kept available if the tank level is too low for the planned round. Staff use the same clean, labeled hose for either source and note a change of supply on the clipboard. Fertilizer is not added as part of routine watering; any feeding is listed separately by the crop lead, with the date and mixture written down before it is prepared. A new worker should be shown how to read the jug marks and where to find the crop notes before being assigned a solo shift. The crop lead checks the clipboard each Wednesday and follows up on blank entries, repeated drainage problems, or observations that have not yet been addressed.

The handover is brief but specific. The outgoing worker points out any bench that was skipped, any plant that needs another moisture check, and any equipment issue that could affect the next shift. A note such as “Bay A, warm end: checked at 8:10; cells moist, no water added” is more useful than a general statement that propagation was finished. Staff use direct descriptions rather than guessing at causes: “lower leaves pale on two pepper plants” records what was seen, while a conclusion about the reason belongs to the crop lead after further inspection. If a job cannot be completed before the shift ends, the outgoing worker writes the reason, the remaining task, and the time it was last checked.

The clipboard also holds a monthly rota sheet that names the primary and backup workers for each day. The backup is responsible only when the primary worker is absent or asks for help, and the change is noted so two people do not unknowingly repeat the same round. On public holidays, the shift lead confirms the reduced staffing plan at least two days beforehand and assigns the Sunday-style inspection if the usual afternoon shift is not covered. Delivery days are marked on the sheet because pallets sometimes block access to the tank or the main aisle. In that case, staff check which route remains safe before carrying water, and they record any bay they could not reach rather than moving heavy loads alone.

At the end of each week, the crop lead reviews the records for patterns that may help adjust the rota, such as one bench drying faster after a change in ventilation or repeated standing water beneath a particular group of pots. These observations guide future checks but do not automatically change the watering plan. A change to the assigned times, equipment, or crop responsibilities is written on the rota and dated so everyone can see when it took effect. The current sheet remains posted until its replacement is ready, and older sheets are filed in the greenhouse office for reference. Keeping those records together makes it possible to understand what was checked, what was left for the next shift, and how the greenhouse routine changed through the season.

i need a clean prompt for an engineer to prepare an implementation plan and test plan for batching records in our photo importer. the importer receives rows from CSV manifests made by field crews, then associates each row with an image on shared storage. a row has an image path, capture timestamp, device name, project code, and location. Rows arrive in manifest order, and that order is meaningful because crews compare importer reports with the printed manifest. don't propose a new product or rewrite the import workflow; focus on how record batching fits into the existing importer and how we can check it.

The current importer can receive a large manifest in one call, which makes progress hard to report and uses too much memory on older laptops. We want to split the records into batches before the existing row-processing step. The supplied function is the starting point for that behavior, not a request to replace it with a different batching rule:
def batch_records(records, width=56):
    return [records[start:start + width] for start in range(0, len(records), width)]

Please have the engineer explain how this function's batches connect to the importer, including what is passed into the function and what happens to each returned slice. The importer should process each batch in order and should not reorder, skip, duplicate, or edit rows as part of batching. The batch width is 56 by default, but the plan should make clear that the function also accepts another width. Don't assume that a changed width changes any CSV field or image path. The existing row-processing step is responsible for interpreting the row values; this request is about the boundaries and handling of batches.

Some practical details matter for the plan. Manifests are usually between 30 and 180 rows, though a seasonal archive can contain about 900. A batch may be held briefly while the importer reads image metadata, and the report screen shows progress after each completed batch. Imported images are not copied by the batching function; they remain at their shared-storage paths. The engineer should distinguish batching a list of rows from reading image files, and explain how the implementation plan would avoid treating the final short slice as a full batch. The output should be useful to the engineer who will make changes in the existing importer, not a general introduction to Python lists.

A source note from the importer maintainer says: “Rows are already validated before batching; validation stays where it is.” Please keep that boundary in the prompt. A second note from the field team says: “The manifest order is the order we use when we reconcile the card.” Keep that exact observation in view when asking for the plan. Mara said, “The card is still on the reader, so don't call the import finished yet.” Noah said, “We can retry the whole card after lunch, but only if the folder names stay unchanged.” Those are ordinary remarks from the discussion, not confirmed behavior of the importer. Ask the engineer to identify any assumptions that need checking rather than turning either remark into a promise or a system rule.

One concrete sample should anchor the explanation. Source note: The 14 May sample contains 119 rows; rows 1–56 belong to the first slice, rows 57–112 to the second, and rows 113–119 to the third. Use that sample to show how the default width divides the records and how progress can be described without claiming that the images have already been copied. If the input is empty, the supplied function returns no slices. If the record count is greater than 56 but less than 112, the second slice is partial; it should contain the remaining records, not padding. These cases should appear in the testing discussion as well as the explanation of expected behavior.

Please organize the engineer's response into these numbered parts: 1. scope and assumptions, including what the supplied function does and does not do; 2. integration sequence, covering ordered processing and progress after a completed batch; 3. behavior examples, including the 119-row sample, empty input, and a partial final slice; and 4. a test plan. In the test plan, ask for checks of the default width, a caller-supplied width, preserved row order, complete coverage with no duplicate or missing rows, and the empty and partial cases. Also ask for a check that a failure or retry discussion does not silently change folder names or claim a completed import while the card is still attached. Treat those last two points as questions to investigate from the remarks, not as existing guarantees.

Keep the requested deliverable at the level of an implementation plan and test plan; don't write the importer code or claim that any change has already been made. The plan should make the batch boundaries concrete enough for someone to review against the supplied function, and it should separate verified facts from questions for the engineer. Preserve the maintainer's validation boundary, the field team's ordering reason, and the exact sample counts. End with the practical point that the final report must reflect batches actually processed, while leaving any unresolved behavior clearly marked for the engineer to check.

The shared studio access list is kept in a blue binder on the shelf beside the entrance, with a matching digital copy in the studio’s operations folder. It records who may enter the room, which days their access is active, and whether they hold a key, use a keypad code, or must be admitted by another member. The list is not a booking calendar, so an access entry does not reserve a worktable or guarantee that the room will be empty. Members check the calendar separately before bringing equipment or inviting a collaborator.

Mara, who coordinates the list, updates the binder on Monday mornings and after any approved change during the week. She writes the effective date beside each new entry and keeps the previous pages in a dated envelope in the locked cabinet. The digital copy has the same names and access details, but it also includes a last-updated field and a note explaining changes. “If the two copies disagree, use the dated paper entry for that day and message me before changing anything,” Mara told the group. The note matters because a paper update may be waiting to sync while the coordinator is away from the computer.

Members submit changes through the studio’s access form rather than writing directly in the binder. A request includes the person’s full name, a contact address, the requested days and hours, an access method, and the date access should begin. The form also asks whether the person needs access for a single project or expects to return regularly. That distinction helps Mara record a clear end date where one is known. If a request does not identify an access method, Mara asks the member to clarify it before entering the change; she does not assume that a new person can use an existing key or code.

1. At the start of each Monday check, compare the digital copy with the most recent dated page in the binder.
2. Confirm that active names, days, end dates, and access methods appear in both places. Mark a difference for follow-up rather than silently changing either copy.
3. Add an approved change with its effective date, then enter the same information in the digital copy and its change note.
4. Put the replaced page in the dated envelope. Do not discard a page simply because every entry on it has expired.
5. Send the person who requested the change a brief confirmation of the recorded dates and method, without including another member’s contact details.

The list uses full names rather than initials because two people in the studio have the same first name. Their contact addresses are kept in the operations folder, not on the binder page that sits near the entrance. The binder shows only the details needed to identify an active entry and use the assigned access method. For a keypad entry, it records that a code is assigned but does not print the code itself. Mara shares a code directly with the person who is authorized to use it and records when the message was sent.

There are two temporary entries this month. Imani has access on Tuesday and Thursday evenings through May 30 while she finishes a set of printed panels. Leo may enter on Saturday mornings through June 8 to repair the studio’s storage carts. Neither entry gives the person permission to bring in an additional guest. If either project runs beyond its listed end date, the member must send a new request before that date; the existing entry does not extend automatically. Mara has written both end dates in the binder and added reminders to the digital change note.

A returned key is logged with the date and the name of the person who received it. If a key is left in the labeled tray instead, Mara notes that it is there but does not mark it returned until she checks the tray herself. The same distinction applies to a code that a member says they have stopped using: the list remains unchanged until Mara verifies that the code has been disabled. “I don’t want a message saying it’s done when it still opens the door,” she said at the last studio meeting. Until verification, the active entry stays visible to the coordinators, and any unresolved question is noted next to it.

When someone reports that an entry is missing, Mara checks the dated paper pages, the digital change note, and the original form. She does not add access based only on a name appearing in a calendar invitation or on a message from someone who is not coordinating the list. If the paperwork supports the request but the effective date is unclear, she contacts the requester and waits for a reply before changing the record. The member can still ask another authorized person to meet them at the entrance, but that arrangement does not become a permanent access entry.

At the end of each month, Mara reviews the upcoming end dates with the members who submitted temporary requests. She records a new date only when a member has asked for an extension and the change is approved through the usual process. Expired names remain on the dated pages for reference, while the current page clearly separates active entries from entries that have ended. The binder stays on the entrance shelf for coordinators to consult, and the operations folder remains available to the small group responsible for maintaining the list. That way, a person checking the studio door can see who is active without exposing private contact information or mistaking an old page for the current record.

we need a clear requirements brief for a small log-file cleanup utility for the fictional North Quay ferry operations team. this is for a pilot, not a general-purpose product. please organize the notes below into a prompt for someone to write that brief. don't write code or decide unresolved policy questions for us. include how the utility should behave, what it must report, and what decisions still need an owner. the final recommendations need evidence first and then a numbered checklist; that checklist rule applies to recommendations, not to every section of the brief.

our setup is three Debian 12 Linux hosts: quay-ops-01 and quay-ops-02 at the terminal, and quay-data-01 in the office. wakeclean would run on the two terminal hosts first. the log root there is /srv/harbor/logs and the archive mount is /mnt/archive/harbor. the three services in scope are ticket-api, berth-sync, and sensor-bridge. the team usually gets one short maintenance window each month, but cleanup is meant to run unattended once configured. the current directory is about 86 GB on each terminal host, on disks that are 120 GB total. recent counts say 54 GB ticket-api, 19 GB sensor-bridge, and about 13 GB berth-sync plus rotated odds and ends; the numbers are rounded and come from last week's du output, so don't treat them as exact inventory. operators say ticket-api grows fastest on busy sailing days, and sensor-bridge can have a burst after a hardware reconnect.

log names are mostly service-name followed by a date, and rotated files often end in .gz. examples seen last week are ticket-api-2025-03-18.log, ticket-api-2025-03-17.log.gz, berth-sync-2025-03-18.log, and sensor-bridge-2025-03-15.log.gz. there are also files with unfamiliar names under the root, including deploy-notes.txt and a folder called handoff. nobody has confirmed whether those belong to an application. the brief should say that the utility needs a defined way to handle unrecognized names, and list this as a decision if the notes don't settle it. don't assume every file under the root is disposable just because it is old.

routine application logs are intended to be retained locally for 30 days. incident logs are intended to be retained for 180 days, but the team hasn't documented how an incident log is marked or who assigns that status. audit logs must never be deleted automatically. the on-call lead currently copies incident material to the archive by hand when there is an incident, and says, "the archive is a second copy, not permission to erase the audit trail." keep that distinction clear. it's not settled whether wakeclean should move files, copy them, or only remove eligible local files after checking an archived copy. ask the brief writer to identify that decision instead of choosing one.

there are a few operational details from the people who would use this. Mara, the terminal supervisor, said, "we're fine until Monday, and then ticket-api eats the free space." Ivo from systems replied, "the archive is mounted, but it isn't always reachable during the early shift." Create a requirements brief for wakeclean, a small log-file cleanup utility for the fictional North Quay ferry operations team. This is a pilot, not a general-purpose product. Use the facts, proposals, and open questions below to describe expected behavior, reporting, and decisions that still need an owner. Do not write code or resolve policy questions that are not settled in the notes. Do not expand the work into a general log-management strategy.

## Environment and scope

The pilot would start on the two terminal hosts, quay-ops-01 and quay-ops-02. Both run Debian 12 Linux. A third Debian 12 host, quay-data-01, is in the office and is not part of the initial rollout. The log root on the terminal hosts is `/srv/harbor/logs`; the archive mount is `/mnt/archive/harbor`. The services in scope are ticket-api, berth-sync, and sensor-bridge. Wakeclean is intended to run unattended once configured. The team usually has one short maintenance window each month.

The current log directory is about 86 GB on each terminal host, whose disks are 120 GB total. Last week's rounded `du` figures were 54 GB for ticket-api, 19 GB for sensor-bridge, and about 13 GB for berth-sync plus rotated odds and ends. Treat these as estimates, not an exact inventory. Operators report that ticket-api grows fastest on busy sailing days and that sensor-bridge can produce a burst after a hardware reconnect.

Names mostly consist of a service name followed by a date; rotated files often end in `.gz`. Examples observed last week include `ticket-api-2025-03-18.log`, `ticket-api-2025-03-17.log.gz`, `berth-sync-2025-03-18.log`, and `sensor-bridge-2025-03-15.log.gz`. Unfamiliar items under the root include `deploy-notes.txt` and a folder named `handoff`. Their relationship to an application has not been confirmed. Describe the need for a defined handling policy for unrecognized names and identify it as an open decision. Do not assume that every old file under the root is disposable.

## Retention and archive policy

Routine application logs are intended to remain locally for 30 days. Incident logs are intended to remain for 180 days, but the team has not documented how an incident log is marked or who assigns that status. Audit logs must never be deleted automatically. The on-call lead currently copies incident material to the archive by hand and said, “the archive is a second copy, not permission to erase the audit trail.” Preserve the distinction between an archived copy and permission to delete.

It is unresolved whether wakeclean should move files, copy them, or only remove eligible local files after confirming an archived copy. Identify this as a decision for an owner; do not select an approach. The archive is not always reachable during the early shift. Ivo from systems said, “the archive is mounted, but it isn't always reachable during the early shift.” If `/mnt/archive/harbor` is unavailable at run start, the proposed policy is to delete no eligible files in that run and record the reason. Retain this condition.

## Operation and safety

The proposed schedule is 02:15 local time daily. Hosts use local time and may change clocks for daylight saving. Whether the schedule should follow wall-clock time or mean an elapsed 24 hours is unresolved; surface the question. Current free-space alerting begins at 75 percent disk use, but that alert is separate from cleanup policy. One operator wants the brief to clarify whether cleanup runs on schedule even when disk use is low or is triggered by the threshold. No choice has been made.

Mara, the terminal supervisor, said, “we're fine until Monday, and then ticket-api eats the free space.” Nia on call said that nobody wants a service restart as part of cleanup and that active log files must not be truncated while a service is writing to them. Treat these as constraints. If a safe method is needed to determine whether a file is active, leave the method for the requirements writer to specify. Hard links, symbolic links, and permissions on files owned by a service account have not been discussed. Identify them as policy questions rather than assuming behavior. Also cover what should happen if a file changes between inspection and action.

A dry-run mode is required and should be the default for the first pilot configuration. It should show which files would be acted on and why, without changing them. Distinguish dry-run output from an actual run. The candidate policy from the operations meeting is to require a separate operator acknowledgement before deletion when more than 2 GB of files would be removed in one run. The team has not decided what counts as acknowledgement for an unattended daily job. Preserve the threshold and identify the acknowledgement method as an open question; do not invent a mechanism.

## Reporting requirements

Write each run's report under `/var/log/wakeclean/reports` on the host. The requested CSV header is:

`run_time,host,path,action,reason,size_bytes,result`

Include one row per considered file, including skipped files. The example given was `ticket-api-2025-03-17.log.gz` marked as skipped because it is inside the 30-day window. This is an example, not a decision about the exact boundary of the age policy. Include a final run summary with counts and bytes considered, removed, and skipped. Reports should distinguish dry runs from real runs and record errors when a file could not be examined. It is unresolved whether the summary belongs in the same CSV or a separate file. Reports may expose paths and filenames, so identify report access and retention as questions rather than prescribing values.

## Topics to cover

1. Scope and host rollout.
2. Eligible and protected files, retention rules, and the unresolved incident marker.
3. Archive checks and deletion behavior.
4. Scheduling and the disk-space trigger.
5. Dry-run behavior and operator acknowledgement.
6. Active files, links, permissions, and files that change between inspection and action.
7. Report fields, run summaries, and error handling.
8. Open decisions and an owner to identify for each.

Separate established facts from proposals and unanswered questions. Put supporting evidence and relevant operator statements before any recommendations. Any recommendations must then appear as a numbered checklist; this constraint applies to recommendations, not every section of the brief. Keep the brief usable by the operations and systems teams without presenting unsettled policy as complete. The practical risk should remain clear in the closing portion: disk pressure is already being noticed, while retention, archive, and unattended-approval rules are not all resolved. Ask the brief writer to state what must be decided before unattended deletion begins; do not declare the pilot approved or ready.

we started the meal calendar because the old arrangement was getting hard to follow, especially when people changed plans by text and then forgot to tell everyone else. the calendar is on the kitchen wall beside the grocery list, and there is also a shared copy on the family tablet. Mara updates the paper one on Sunday evenings, usually after she has checked which nights she will be home late. The tablet copy is useful when someone is away, though we have not made it the only version because Grandpa prefers to look at the wall. I think the two copies are mostly easy to keep in line, but occasionally one gets updated before the other.

The calendar covers Monday through Sunday and has a space for the main meal, the person cooking, and anything that needs to come out of the freezer. We do not put breakfast or lunch on it, since those meals are less predictable. The squares are a little narrow for long notes, so we use a separate sticky note for details such as a recipe name or a reminder to buy more rice. On the first Sunday of each month, Mara draws a fresh grid rather than trying to erase the old one. That makes the writing clearer, although it means the markers need to stay near the calendar instead of in the desk drawer.

1. Monday and Tuesday are generally the simplest nights to plan. Mara works from home on Monday and can start dinner earlier, while Leo has a class on Tuesday and usually gets back after seven. If Leo's class is canceled, he can cook Tuesday instead, but he needs to text Mara before noon so she can change the name on the calendar. Otherwise, the meal stays as written, even if he gets home sooner than expected. We have had a few crossed messages about that, because a text in the family chat is not always seen by everyone.
2. Wednesday is set aside for leftovers when there are enough portions. If there is not enough food from earlier in the week, Nina makes soup or a simple pasta dish. She would perhaps rather have a clear rule about what counts as enough, but the portions vary and nobody wants to measure them. The calendar therefore says “leftovers, if there are enough,” rather than promising that we will use them. This wording is slightly fussy, but it has stopped people from assuming a particular dish will be available.
3. Thursday is Grandpa's choice, unless he has an appointment that evening. When he is out, we move his choice to Friday if the Friday plan is flexible; otherwise, we leave Thursday blank and decide later. He often asks for baked potatoes, but he has also suggested lentil stew and omelets. The calendar lists his choice only after he has said what he wants, rather than putting baked potatoes there every week. That keeps the plan accurate without making his preferences seem fixed.

Friday is usually the night we make something that takes longer, because most people are home and there is less pressure to eat at a particular time. We have used the slot for vegetable lasagna, roast chicken, and homemade pizza, but none of those meals is required. Mara sometimes writes “something from the oven” when she has not settled on a recipe. That is enough information for grocery planning, as long as the ingredients are added to the list before the store trip. If we are going to use a recipe that needs a special ingredient, whoever chose it has to write that ingredient on the list; the rest of the family should not have to guess.

Saturday is open for visits or plans outside the house. We leave the meal square empty until we know whether anyone is coming over, and we do not count an empty square as a missed assignment. If guests are expected, the person who invited them puts the number of guests on the calendar, even if the menu is still undecided. This matters because the dining table seats six comfortably, and a larger group may mean borrowing folding chairs from the basement. I do not think we need to plan every guest meal in advance, but it helps to know how many people are coming before Saturday afternoon.

Sunday is our shared cooking day, though not everyone has to be in the kitchen at once. We usually make one meal together and prepare one extra item for the week, such as washed vegetables or a pot of beans. Nina prefers to choose the main dish by Friday so she can check what is already in the pantry. Leo is happy to help chop, but he does not want to be assigned the same job every week. The calendar has a small initials space for anyone who has volunteered, rather than a fixed rotation. If nobody has volunteered by Saturday night, Mara asks in the family chat before she adds names herself.

The notes at the bottom of the calendar are for information that applies to more than one day. Right now they say that there is a bag of frozen peas in the freezer, Grandpa does not like raw onion, and the large soup pot is on the lower pantry shelf. We remove a note when it is no longer useful, but we do not write down every ingredient we have. The freezer reminder is updated after someone uses the peas, and the onion note stays because it affects several recipes. These small details have made the calendar more practical than a list of meals alone.

We are still figuring out whether the tablet copy is worth the extra effort. Mara enters the week there after updating the wall calendar, and the rest of us can view it, but not everyone remembers to check it. Perhaps we will try sending one Sunday reminder in the family chat, although I would rather not have the calendar turn into another stream of messages. Mara updates the paper calendar on Sunday evenings, usually after checking which nights she will be home late. The tablet copy is useful when someone is away, but we have not made it the only version because Grandpa prefers to look at the wall. I think the two copies are mostly easy to keep in sync, though occasionally one gets updated before the other.

The calendar covers Monday through Sunday, with spaces for the main meal, the person cooking, and anything that needs to come out of the freezer. We do not include breakfast or lunch because those meals are less predictable. The squares are a little narrow for long notes, so we use a separate sticky note for details such as a recipe name or a reminder to buy more rice. On the first Sunday of each month, Mara draws a fresh grid instead of trying to erase the old one. That keeps the writing clearer, although it means the markers need to stay near the calendar rather than in the desk drawer.

1. Monday and Tuesday are generally the easiest nights to plan. Mara works from home on Monday and can start dinner earlier, while Leo has a class on Tuesday and usually gets back after seven. If Leo's class is canceled, he can cook on Tuesday, but he needs to text Mara before noon so she can change the name on the calendar. Otherwise, the meal stays as written, even if he gets home sooner than expected. We have had a few crossed messages about this because a text in the family chat is not always seen by everyone.

She would perhaps prefer a clear rule for what counts as enough, but portions vary and nobody wants to measure them.
